This improvement yields a significant boost in computational efficiency, enabling the practical application of coupling layers in complex-valued neural networks for real-world tasks. Our innovative technique utilizes a real-valued Monte Carlo method in combination with a complex-valued deterministic approach, and we demonstrate the benefits of this method in a sample coupling layer network. Furthermore, this development empowers the utilization of Monte Carlo methods in contexts where coupling layers are critically important, such as in the simulation of Markov processes and neural manifolds. Our team explores this concept in a setup with a reduced mean squared error objective and finds that it outperforms the existing, more computationally expensive real-valued Monte Carlo method. Our efficient Monte Carlo algorithm and results can be applied to various processes and networks, making it a valuable contribution to the field. By analyzing this connection, we derive a formula that expresses the total number of spheres as a product of certain factors, which are derived from the parameters of the Coxeter system as a whole, rather than individual reflections. Consequently, this enables us to establish a straightforward computational approach for determining the number of spheres within a specific branch of the stratification, denoted as the weak order of a particular group element. Moreover, our study also provides an infinite number of Coxeter systems, each featuring distinct characteristics, with the common property of possessing infinitely many spheres within their weak order stratification. We investigate how precursor characteristics, location details, and time-sensitive diffusion affect the spread of rumors through a mathematical model. By analyzing a compartmental system with interconnected populations, we determine the model's equilibrium points and adjacent curve characteristics. This enables us to classify the stability of equilibrium points and location-specific equilibrium points as either stable or unstable based on precursor peak and attenuation levels. Furthermore, we employ numerical methods to examine the effects of time-dependent variables on the model. The results are graphically represented through simulations. The analysis and numerical experiments can serve as foundational frameworks for evaluating policy interventions aimed at controlling the spread of misinformation. The stability conditions we derived hold value across various application domains, including the diffusion of hate groups, infectious diseases, and environmental contamination. The specific precursor features and model variations we analyzed are crucial for understanding the problem domain, as illustrated with examples of actual hate groups. The stability of the model has implications for evaluating policy interventions in the following ways: If a rumor reaches the peak before spreading to other locations, increasing the attention devoted to it will cause it to collapse, whereas delaying this response may result in the rumor spreading to other locations and becoming harder to extinguish. Additionally, the model reveals that paying close attention to small precursor peaks can backfire, as this attention itself accelerates the peak's transition to the unstable state and the attendant attenuation coefficient. Consequently, the optimal policy intervention would be to divert attention from small precursor peaks to those that are larger, as these are more likely to produce a significant impact when addressed. The impact of location-specific attention is more complex, as it depends on the distribution of populations across different locations. The model yields the following results: If a particular group is largely geographically isolated, increasing the attention devoted to it will accelerate its peak and attenuation coefficients. In contrast, if the group is widely dispersed across different locations, the optimal policy would be to divert attention from it to other groups, as this will slow down the peak and attenuation coefficients of that particular group. The effectiveness of time-dependent variables on the model is illustrated with an example of a hate group that spread rapidly during the post-election period but was significantly reduced in popularity after the election. The results show that the model accurately replicates the actual time-dependent diffusion pattern of this hate group. The robustness of the model is validated through the application of different parameter estimation methods, as well as the implementation of varying model specifications. We present \textit{LifeStream}, a meta optimizer developed to automatically generate high-performance numerical libraries for stream processors by merely providing access to their API. Stream processors possess exceptional throughput for handling extensive datasets, yet their limited memory hinders them from accomplishing complex computations. To overcome this, we crafted \textit{LifeStream} to efficiently process numerous datasets comprising numerical data by utilizing approximately 5MB of memory. The creator of \textit{LifeStream} employs subtle shortcuts and workarounds to streamline computations, enabling it to surpass conventional hand-optimized numerical libraries in terms of performance. Our findings show \textit{LifeStream} outperforms leading hand-optimized numerical libraries such as NumPy, CoreNumpy, and Half, achieving a significant speedup of 20-50 times when processing various real-world datasets comprising up to 10 million floating point numbers. Furthermore, it surpasses embedded optimized numerical libraries like VECOPA, a contender in the EEMBC Numerics Benchmark, by an impressive margin of 5-10 times. By fixing specific network components, our studies show that, in natural image classification, a large KL Divergence loss can lead to poor performance, whereas a smaller loss like the cross-entropy loss yields better results. Additionally, we successfully applied this technique to a challenging real-world problem, fixing a pre-trained ResNet-50 to adapt it to medical image classification, and observed improved results when using the cross-entropy loss over the standard softmax loss. We also present a straightforward yet effective solution, simply adjusting the learning rate, which significantly enhances performance in both evaluated datasets. This study develops a thermomechanical model that accounts for the solidification of polymers resulting from mechanical stretching. The proposed framework is a nonlinear, viscoelastic formulation that includes specific mechanisms of material degradation and crystallization, and it ensures positive entropy values throughout the process. The model's key feature is the introduction of a surface energy factor that enables the simulation of the formation of crystalline surfaces within the material. Furthermore, the model incorporates the influence of mechanical forces on entropy changes and chemical potential differences. Numerical implementation based on finite elements is also presented and put to use in validating the model through numerical experiments. The study demonstrates the model's capabilities in reproducing the effects of strain-induced crystallization on material density, chemical potential, and the distribution of crystalline and amorphous phases within the material. The role of surface energy in driving the formation of crystalline surfaces is also illustrated. The model is shown to accurately simulate the processes of nucleation and growth of crystalline surfaces as well as the breakup of these surfaces due to mechanical forces. The study highlights the importance of accounting for surface energies and the curvature of the crystalline interface in estimating material densities. The model's limitations are discussed, and future directions, such as incorporating multiple crystalline phases and investigating long-term material solidification, are proposed. The developed code is made available for the scientific community to use and modify. The study's findings demonstrate the capability of viscoelastic models to capture the complex mechanical properties of polymers resulting from strain-induced solidification, and it highlights the importance of considering surface energies and curvature in estimating material densities. The research underpins the development of numerical tools capable of simifying material degradation and the formation of interfaces within polymers resulting from mechanical stretching. The model's applications extend to the simulation of degradation in polymer composites, the formation of interface defects, and the mechanical properties of polymer melts and solutions. The code is suitable for large-scale simulations required for the study of material solidification on a microscale and has been tested on high-performance computing systems. The thermodynamic properties of a physical system in constant pressure conditions are examined to determine the validity of the grand canonical ensemble. Based on the isothermal compressibility, we establish a criterion for the ensemble's validity: the variation in the number of particles must be minimal (i.e., the system should not exhibit significant fluctuations in the number of particles) for the grand canonical ensemble to be applicable. Furthermore, we analyze the conditions under which the canonical and grand canonical ensembles are equivalent. The utility of these ensemble equivalences is demonstrated through applications to ideal gas and van der Waals fluid models. The HHL algorithm is the most efficient known quantum algorithm for solving certain linear systems and matrix equations, but its implementation is hindered by the need to negatively sample from the qubit state and integrate the quantity of interest over the solution space. The limitations of near-surface quantum hardware make this challenge even more significant. To overcome this and enhance the execution of the HHL variant on quantum devices, we developed the NISQ-HHL algorithm, which modifies the original HHL algorithm to enable the solution for matrix equations where one matrix has an inverse that can be efficiently classically computed. This modification allows us to directly measure relevant solutions when the qubit state is successfully created, eliminating the need for destructive measurement and repeated execution. As a result, NISQ-HHL yields a significant improvement (thousands to millions of times) in computational efficiency compared to the conventional HHL algorithm when executing linear systems and matrix equations on quantum devices. The enhanced algorithm is particularly beneficial for applications involving nonlinear optimization, dynamic programming, and reinforcement learning, and we demonstrate its advantages using a random linear system and a real-world dataset. The code for NISQ-HHL has been openly shared to facilitate the quantum-assisted learning for nonlinear models and other related applications. The implementation is compatible with major quantum simulation platforms, including Qiskit and Cirq. The NISQ-HHL algorithm has the potential to be an invaluable tool for the development of quantum-assisted machine learning, especially for nonlinear models and related tasks, and serves as a benchmark for the performance improvement that future quantum hardware can achieve with linear systems and matrix equations. The code for NISQ-HHL, the accompanying benchmark, and the related research have been made publicly available to facilitate the advancement of quantum machine learning. Researchers found a surprising ability in individual nanowire transducers to adjust their superconducting boundary based on the direction of a small voltage applied perpendicular to the current. This adaptation can be significant, amounting to a $10^{-4}$ eV change in the energy barrier, and depends uniquely on the applied voltage's polarity. This peculiar behavior's mechanism is well-explained by a theoretical model that considers the influence of the applied voltage on the nanowire's electrostatic potential and the resulting shape of the energy spectrum. Furthermore, this model demonstrates that the energy barrier's shift can be adjusted by the applied voltage in a way that its sign reverses with a polarity change. If the energy barrier's shift is set within the $10^{-4}$ eV range, it is possible to adjust the nanowire sensor's threshold even more precisely by combining the applied voltage with a magnetic field, resulting in a magnetic tuning capability of about 10^-6 eV/fT. This level of precision is sufficiently small to address the nanowire sensor's threshold even in the presence of electromagnetic interference. Using a quark-diquark picture of baryons, we reinterpret the dynamics of constituent quarks to describe the mass spectra of baryon resonances. This approach, based on the Fock state expansion of a relativized harmonic oscillator, allows us to explain the patterns of mass levels for ground state and excited configurations of both mesons and baryons. We apply this quark-diquark picture to calculate the mass spectra of meson and baryon states, both with and without a harmonic oscillator potential, and compare these calculations to experimental data for mesons and commonly accepted values for baryons. We also generate predictions for missing mass levels of mesons and baryons based on their known counterparts. Hints of a harmonic oscillator pattern in quark dynamics are discussed in the context of multiquark states of exotic charm and the need for quark interactions that comply with the rules of quantum mechanics. We propose experimental studies of recently discovered charmed meson states, such as the $D_{s1}(2536)$ and $B_{1}(5727)$ barions, with possible modes of production that could reveal the nature of these exotic configurations of quarks. We also suggest that many observed meson resonances do not meet the requirements of being true quark states and could be explained by dynamics of hadron interactions similar to molecular orbital theory used in chemistry. Finally, we propose that many missing mass levels of both mesons and baryons could be explained by quark compositions of type diquark-antiquark or three-quark with excited or alternative configurations of those found in ground state configurations. For example, researchers found that in a model representing a well-mixed room, the aerosol virus concentration would quickly reach a stable yet inaccurate equilibrium, significantly overestimating the actual concentration. However, with the addition of simple flow dynamics, the model more accurately reflects more complex simulations, even when they include turbulent airflow. Furthermore, by analyzing these models from a numerical perspective, scientists can enhance their predictive power by accounting for variables like aerosol size and the speed at which they settle. By refining these models, researchers aim to make more precise predictions about the concentration of aerosols around an infected individual over time. Moreover, these models can be applied to various closed settings, such as public transportation or offices, by introducing flow dynamics that reflect the movement of air and aerosols within these spaces. By evaluating these models against actual data from experiments, scientists can ensure their accuracy before utilizing them in future scenarios. By simulating epidemics within these closed spaces over time, researchers have found that aerosol transmissions can contribute significantly to the spread of a virus, especially within confined areas with low ventilation, and that reducing aerosol transmissions through improved ventilation or social distancing measures can significantly slow the spread of an epidemic. Moreover, these models have shown that even a small reduction in aerosol transmissions per day can lead to a substantial decrease in new infections over a longer period, demonstrating the importance of considering aerosol transmissions in the context of epidemics within closed spaces. The Hall effect in Cobalt/Bismuth multilayers has been investigated. By analyzing the scattering mechanism, we found that Bismuth layers at the interface with Cobalt layers do not scatter electrons as effectively as those within the bulk of the Bismuth layers. This reduced scattering is attributed to the alignment of electron spins, which minimizes resistivity in the multilayers. By varying the Bismuth layer thickness, we observed two scattering mechanisms: one where the Hall voltage is resistant to changes in current and another regime where it isn't. In the latter regime, the Hall voltage is resistant to changes in thickness of the Bismuth layers. We also found that the spin alignment leads to an increase in the Anomalous Hall resistance in the multilayers. Notably, this resistance exceeds that of single Cobalt layers, potentially making multilayers suitable for use in spin-based applications. The Anomalous Hall resistance in the multilayers can be adjusted by varying the thickness of the Bismuth layers, offering a promising pathway to developing adjustable spin-based devices. The exact mechanism governing the Anomalous Hall effect in Cobalt/Bismuth multilayers remains unclear and requires further investigation, but it presents a novel and adjustable resistant effect that could be valuable for developing robust and versatile spin-based devices. The results we obtained also suggest that the Anomalous Hall effect in multilayers is influenced by the alignment of electron spins and could potentially serve as a reliable means of creating spin-based devices with adjustable resistance. The exact relationship between the Anomalous Hall effect and the Bismuth layer thickness needs to be explored in greater depth, but it offers a promising foundation for developing spin-based devices with adjustable resistance that are resilient to a range of temperatures and layer thicknesses. The robustness of the Anomalous Hall effect in these multilayers, combined with the ease of fabricating Bismuth layers, make them an attractive choice for developing robust and adjustable spin-based devices with minimal dependence on layer thickness. The Anomalous Hall effect in these multilayers can be adjusted by altering the thickness of the Bismuth layers, offering a novel solution for developing devices with precise adjustable resistance that are less susceptible to the effects of layer thickness. We investigate how the $p$-norm used in a neural network affects its performance when subject to a maximum Lipschitz constant. Previous research demonstrated that limiting the Lipschitz constant can prevent overfitting, prompting our $p$-norm analysis to ensure generalization across datasets. Our study utilizes a theoretical model to demonstrate that the $p$-norm influencing the Lipschitz constant is directly related to the spectral norm of the network's weight matrices. We further find that the optimal $p$ value lies between 1 and 2, depending on the network's size and training data set. Our findings highlight the benefits of employing the matrix norm instead of the vector $p$-norm for neural networks. We also provide practical constraints on the Lipschitz constant and normalisation of output, leading to a normalized network and a utility maximization framework. Our results demonstrate that the optimal $p$ value varies with network size and dataset size, providing a robust approach to ensuring generalisability across different datasets. We validate our approach using multiple datasets, revealing improved performance when employing the matrix norm. This paper describes a NLO+PS generator for vector leptoquarks that efficiently models top and bottom quark production in the LHC via the first generation of leptoquark doublets. Our approach leverages the NLO QCD cross-section and differential jet distributions at the level of partons for the most prevalent hadronic configurations. To minimize computational requirements, we employ a mixture of analytical and numerical components for the cross-section and differential distributions. By activating the 4-particle smooth parton harness (4PS), we mitigate distortions caused by the integration of parton distributions at the tree level. Our generator, VLFrames, can be integrated into existing frameworks like MadGraph5\_aMC@NLO and is capable of producing accurate NLO signal predictions for MESSMER, a multi-purpose search algorithm developed by the ATLAS collaboration. By comparing our generator with existing NLO QCD simulations using LEPTO, we find that it achieves a NLO effective cross-section accuracy of approximately 10^-3 for vector leptoquark masses exceeding 300 GeV. Moreover, our generator demonstrates compatibility with Snowmass 2021 recommendations for efficient NLO signal generation in hadron colliders. Ultimately, VLFrames provides a versatile NLO+PS generator for searching vector leptoquarks within a specific mass range, and its efficiency can be further enhanced via a proposed reweighting technique. Our generator is an useful tool for discovering vector leptoquarks in the top and bottom quark channels of the LHC using NLO QCD standards. Our research also highlights the NLO+PS methodology's potential advantages and proposed refinements for addressing scaling issues and improving efficiency. Our search scenarios for vector leptoquarks are available at https://github.com/VectorLeptoquarks/VLFramesScenarios. A novel deep-neural-network (DNN) framework is proposed for reducing PET noise, leveraging concurrent MRI data to guide the training and implement adaptive image refinement.  Initially, a U-Net-based DNN is developed to learn the transformation for PET image reconstruction from few-view and sparse data.  To further enhance performance and expand applicability, a separate DNN is trained to predict MRI-induced appearance features, which are incorporated into the PET image refinement network, enabling it to focus on detailing noisy PET images rather than learning elemental features.  To facilitate training and model versatility, a U-Net architecture is chosen for both DNNs.  The proposed framework is evaluated through a retrospective analysis of 15 PET/MRI scans acquired during clinical protocols, with results showing that the proposed method surpasses traditional approaches in PET image refinement, achieving a 42.5% increase in structural similarity index and a 24.4% reduction in mean squared error compared to deep learning-based PET reconstruction from sparse data alone.  Furthermore, the proposed framework demonstrates robust performance across varying MRI contrast types and acquisition times, cementing its value as a promising technique for noise-reduced PET imaging.  The implemented code and research data are available for public use on GitHub and GitHub, respectively.  Future directions for this research involve exploring alternative DNN architectures, incorporating temporal information for dynamic PET scans, and adapting the framework for low-dose CT and positron emission tomography (PET) combinations.  The proposed noise-reduced PET imaging method has been made available to the scientific community through an open-access license, encouraging widespread utilization and further development by external researchers. This study examines how contextualized language models affect the performance of neural coreference resolution models in relation to centering theory. Specifically, we analyze the impact of BERT and SPACE on coreference properties identified in centering theory, investigating 13 properties and analyzing 15 different models. Our findings show that neural coreference models with the highest accuracy scores do not necessarily perform best in terms of coreference properties, and some even perform poorly. We also discover inconsistencies in the expected distribution of coreference properties, which we attribute to the influence of contextualized embeddings. Our research highlights the potential for further improvement in neural coreference resolution models and highlights the utility of centering theory as a benchmark for coreference properties. We have made the data and code for this study available at https://github.com/zhuyong5/neural-coref-centering. We investigated the impact of surface curvature on homogenous polymer brushes anchored at multiple points, specifically looking at how it affects their free energy due to stretching. This investigation applied to polymer brushes attached to the surface of nanoparticles, micelles, and other curved surfaces was carried out through simulations of looped brush samples using molecular dynamics with non-bond interactions, and the results were verified through simulations of single polymer chains. By examining the free energy associated with stretching, we found that it increases with the inverse square of the surface curvature, and this phenomenon has been explained through the analysis of force distribution within the brush. Furthermore, we observed that the equilibrium distance between grafted polymers on a curved surface is less than expected, and this distance follows an inverse relationship with the surface tension, well beyond the point where the brush thickness equals the equilibrium distance. Additionally, we discovered that the free energy of stretching is directly proportional to the number of grafted polymers, the surface tension, and the inverse of the surface curvature, and it also depends on the mass and distribution of force within the brush. Lastly, we established that the mass of force within the brush falls within the range 1.5 to 2.5, remaining relatively constant across different brush densities and curvatures. The successful verification of these findings through single-chain simulations ensured their validity even in the absence of chain-chain interactions. The analytical expression obtained can be utilized in the scaling analysis of brush geometry and free energy, making it a significant step towards understanding the complex behavior of polymer brushes in curved surfaces. The remaining questions and uncertainties surrounding the effect of surface curvature on polymer brushes have been identified, and the limitations of the current research have been determined to be primarily related to the lack of consideration for inhomogeneous brushes and brushes in the presence of strong forces, as well as the need for further verification of the force distribution analysis in the middle brush region. The method used in this research, MD-SLLO, has been created as a new simulation tool with novel features, including non-bond interactions, looped brush samples, and single-chain simulations, and it has been made publicly available. The data generated during this research have been deposited into public repositories, and the simulation code has been deposited into a code repository. The research has been conducted in compliance with ethical standards, and the authors have declared no conflicts of interest. Given a graph G = (V, E), the geodesic distance between two vertices i, j is the fewest number of edges in a path between i and j. If we truncate this distance to a value k, we get a new graph G_k, consisting of vertices that are within a geodesic distance of k, and edges connecting vertices that are a geodesic distance of 1 or k from each other. We find that for k ≥ 1, the metric dimension of G_k is less than or equal to min{|V| - k, √(2|V| - 2)} and for k ≥ 2, the metric dimension of G_k is greater than or equal to (k - 1)/2. Furthermore, we can determine the exact metric dimension of G_k for k = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. We also provide lower and upper bounds for these values of k. Interestingly, the metric dimension of G_k is not simply k + 1 for any k, as one might intuitively expect. We conclude by exploring the relationship between the metric dimension of G_k and a related concept known as the k-geodesic domi-nance. We discover that they are equivalent for k = 1 and 2, but distinct for k ≥ 3. We hope our findings pave the way for further study into these intricate ideas. Active galactic nuclei (AGNs) vary significantly in luminosity in different wavelengths and observing time frames, with some exhibiting consistent behaviors through extensive periods of observation, while others require longer-term analysis to reveal periodic patterns, pronounced variations, or steady states. However, the bulk of multi-wavelength AGN variability studies is hampered by observing time frames that are too brief for certain sources, and reliance on single-telescope data that can limit broad-band coverage, even with the use of long observation records. We used extensive X-ray and optical data from the 10-m point source observer (PSO) with observations spanning up to nine years to analyze the variability of 53 high-luminosity quasars, including the effects of looking at the same time intervals with different wavelengths, examining optical spectra for correlations with variability, and searching for long-period variations in luminosity. We observed that looking at the same time intervals with different wavelengths reveals different patterns of variability, especially when considering shorter time frames, while there is no clear correlation between optical luminosity and the amplitude of variability when examining large time frames, and only a weak correlation when examining shorter time frames, along with no significant correlation with the slope of the X-ray spectrum or optical energy distribution. Additionally, we found that while some sources exhibit long-period variations in luminosity, these periods are generally longer than the observed period of PSO, and other factors like random fluctuations and looking at the same time intervals with different wavelengths might influence these variations. We also used the X-ray and optical data to calculate the bolometric luminosity of the sources and the energy closure fraction in the X-ray and optical bands, along with the fraction of variability in the X-ray band, but were unable to determine the mechanisms of variability or the masses of the central black holes with the available data. We presented the data in useful formats for the scientific community to analyze the variability of AGNs over extensive time frames, along with recommendations for future observations that could provide more detailed variability analysis by targeting specific variables like the masses of the central black holes, the mechanisms of variability, and the characteristics of periodic patterns, along with considering different looking times in different wavelengths and examining the variability in the optical spectra. We published the X-ray and optical data, along with the analysis, in the form of papers and supplementary materials that are accessible through the PSO website. We also released the software used for the analysis, along with guidelines for using the software, on the website of the X-ray Data Analysis Software website. In the context of cooperative decision-making, where agents have diverse preferences, determining a stable and efficient collaboration is complicated. To simplify this problem, researchers often employ valuation functions that can be compared using matchings in bipartite graphs and directed networks. However, recent studies have shown that these functions may result in significantly inferior approximations of social welfare, potentially as low as 1/2. This paper delves into two related problems: finding the minimum number of binary preference comparisons required to ensure a specific approximation bound for social welfare and determining the maximum possible approximation when comparisons are unbounded. A key contribution of this work is introducing a novel approach that utilizes directed network matchings to solve these problems, thereby highlighting the limitations of current algorithms based on bipartite matchings. The results demonstrate that when comparisons are binary, an approximation of at least 3/4 is impossible to achieve, although it is possible to achieve an approximation of 4/5 when comparisons are unbounded. Furthermore, the paper introduces two notable applications of these problems, demonstrating their relevance in forecasting collective decisions and evaluating the robustness of collaborative systems. The approach developed here can be adapted for additional problem variations and offers a framework for addressing related challenges in the field of cooperative decision-making. The existing algorithm based on bipartite matchings was found to be insufficient and has been superseded by a more efficient algorithm consisting of only two lines of code, providing a marked improvement, especially when comparing the computational efficiency in scenarios with large numbers of agents. The paper's findings have implications for the efficient computation of social welfare in cooperative decision-making settings with restricted valuations, offering a concise and efficient solution that can be utilized as a baseline for comparing the performance of more complex algorithms in the field. The research mentioned in this paper has been previously published in the 30th International Conference on Distributed Computing and the 18th Conference on Web and Internet Mining, respectively, and is incorporated into this paper as a continuation of that work. The paper's results regarding the approximation of social welfare have been shown to be inherently robust, given the limitations of valuations, and as such, the definitions and results have been found applicable to diverse cooperative decision-making scenarios, including but not restricted to multiagent resource allocation, public sector economics, and healthcare systems. The paper also explores the relationship between the comparison of valuations and the concept of resilience in cooperative decision-making, demonstrating its relevance to forecasting collective decisions and evaluating the robustness of collaborative systems, before concluding with the potential avenues for future research in this area. These methods leverage the variations in a object's image properties resulting from both its motion and binarity, allowing us to determine the astrometric closure quantity ($\Delta C$) and assess an object's likelihood of being binary ($P_b$). These techniques are applied to pre-existing survey data for main belt asteroids (MBAs), employing images from multiple fields of view, and considering various factors like asteroid motion, resolution, signal-to-noise ratio, and field of view. The resulting $P_b$ probability distributions serve as inputs for binary asteroid detection models, and after evaluating 693 randomly selected MBA targets, we found that 1.42% of them meet the binary criteria, mapped to the shape parameter $\lambda = 0.25$. If the entire population of MBA asteroids with diameters greater than 100 km is considered, our estimated binary population fraction is 0.84%, also obtained from the OSIRIS-REx sample, and is consistent with previous findings. However, for larger asteroids (D > 500 km), the fraction of binaries is significantly higher, at 13.75%, and this value could be higher due to detection limitations. Our study highlights key factors influencing asteroid binary detection, including their orientation, orbital period, and mass ratio, and also highlights the need for future surveys with higher resolution images, improved astrometric precision, and larger field of view optics. We conducted an investigation to demystify the effectiveness of cooperative game-playing AI that follows a theory-of-mind (ToM), which enables agents to infer others' intentions and maintain shared mental representations. ToM research, particularly within cognitive science, has long suggested its benefits for cooperative behavior, yet the exact mechanism by which ToM facilitates cooperation in games remains unclear. To address this knowledge gap, we developed a ToM-based approach that takes into account the internal states of others in a way that is relevant to achieving cooperative goals. To test and validate our ToM approach, we utilized the 'Bubble Puzzle' cooperative domain as an example case. In the 'Bubble Puzzle', two agents work together to resolve a problem by managing bubbles in a grid. Our results indicate that incorporating a ToM approach enhances the success of the agents in achieving their goals compared to an exclusionary focus on individual objectives. Furthermore, our research revealed that ToM AI excels in situations characterized by uncertainty, changes in context, and a lack of shared knowledge. Finally, our ToM approach was found to be beneficial even in scenarios where other optimal solutions existed, demonstrating its specificity to situations rather than providing a generally 'over-engineered' solution. We also gathered empirical evidence to illustrate that the positive impact of ToM AI is attributable to its capacity to manage mental state inferences, rather than other underlying mechanisms such as attention or problem-solving capabilities. Our research contributes to the understanding of ToM AI in a cognitive context by showcasing its applicability to a broad range of cognitive tasks that are inherently cooperative in nature. We also introduced several novel cognitive tests tailored to assessing ToM capabilities in a way that is relevant to the underlying mechanisms of ToM AI. Ultimately, our research paves the way for further exploration of the relationship between ToM AI and cognitive properties through the development of a unified theoretical framework that integrates both ToM AI and cognitive ToM properties within a single, coherent structure. We also made the code for our ToM approach and cognitive tests publicly available to foster ongoing research in this area. We strongly believe that sharing our code and research will facilitate the advancement of our understanding of ToM AI and its capabilities within a cognitive context, as well as its potential applications in real-world settings. A knotted protein is characterized by a non-trivial trefoil knot within its chain, and the distinction between shallow and deep knotted refers to the point at which the knot is formed during folding. Our research discovers that the folding pathway of shallow knotted proteins involves an initial formation of native contacts in multiple segments before they cross over to create the knotted structure, a process unlike which deeply knotted proteins form the knot immediately after initial folding. Our studies also uncover specific patterns of the single-domain shallow knotted protein, including how they resist unfolding through misfolding, compared to their deeply knotted counterparts. Moreover, our findings suggest that the unique folding pattern of the E. coli dihydrofolate reductase protein is an exception rather than a rule among shallow knotted proteins. Our algorithm's effectiveness is evaluated through the recovery of known knotted protein structures and comparison with alternative methods of trefoil knot recognition. Given a symplectic manifold, we investigate how altering an irrational condition on its symplectic form influences the manifold's topological characteristics. Specifically, we focus on 4-dimensional symplectic manifolds with an irrational $\omega$-filling property and irrational circle invariant curves. Our main achievement is to demonstrate that under these assumptions, the manifold cannot be approximated by rational symplectic structures. Furthermore, we establish the invariance of its symplectic type under a $C^0$-approach to rational structures. Additionally, we prove the existence of a $C^0$-norm on the space of symplectic structures on the manifold, which is analogous to the $C^0$-norm used to characterize the space of irrational flows on a torus. Lastly, we investigate this norm's relationship to the minimum algebraic area of closed curves under a $C^0$-variation. Moreover, we observe that it satisfies the Cauchy's criterion, indicating that it defines a distance metric. However, it does not satisfy the triangle inequality and thus is not a standard metric. We also discover that this norm can be used to demonstrate the distinctness of certain symplectic types that cannot be distinguished using classical means. Ultimately, our research reveals a connection between the irrationality of a symplectic structure and the minimum algebraic area of closed curves under a $C^0$-variation, which we believe is worthy of further exploration. We are also able to establish the existence of a unique optimal symplectic structure on the Klein bottle with respect to a specific property, which we term "irrational $\omega$-filling", and demonstrate that this structure cannot be approximated by rational symplectic structures. We have also discovered that this unique structure has a $C^0$-norm of infinity, whereas all other Klein bottles have a $C^0$-norm of zero. Our research proposes the DISCO framework to enhance both machine learning models' robustness and generalization capabilities. Counterfactual data is generated using a text generation technique and augmented training data, and we demonstrate the benefits of this approach in classification tasks. Specifically, we find that using counterfactual data generated in the 'intention' behind specific predictions significantly improves model performance in counterfactual outcomes as measured by the Counterfactual Generalization Assessment. Moreover, this method shows promise in augmenting data for robustness and generalization, surpassing traditional data augmentation methods. Our proposed DISCO framework is versatile and applicable to various tasks and datasets, additionally showcasing counterfactual data's benefits in evaluating machine learning models' fairness. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghdng/disco-fg. Our proposed method, the paper suggests, provides a meaningful counterfactual generalization assessment and enhances machine learning performance, leading to a promising avenue for further research. Our analysis and results are detailed in the paper, along with concrete guidelines for implementing the proposed method in various contexts. This work proposes a novel deep learning framework that leverages information from side streams to improve the detection of cardiac abnormalities in noisy echocardiogram images. The proposed model includes three components: a central encoder that generates a compressed, high-level image description; and two side streams, each processing a distinct type of noise, that produce noise-specific features and a noise indicator for the majority voting process. The integrated framework employs two techniques to enhance detection performance: it conducts majority voting on the noise indicator for each sample and employs noise-specific features in the fusion of the central and side streams representations. Utilizing DIPF, a deep learning-based approach to filter noisy images, we developed a training protocol that removes noise from training data and applied it to detect cardiac systolic dysfunction in noisy echocardiogram images. The results demonstrate that the proposed model outperforms conventional techniques, including U-Net, both in the presence and absence of noise. Specifically, with noise, the proposed model achieves a higher detection performance than U-Net in all metrics (Sens, Spec, ACC) and reduces standard U-Net's performance metric values by 0.31, 0.24, and 0.27 in the presence of noise. Additionally, the proposed model demonstrates comparable performance to clean data when evaluating on echocardiogram images without noise. Medical research institutions and organizations are increasingly using federated learning to analyze health data, where a server collaborates with client devices to develop machine learning models without accessing their raw data. However, activity recognition using wearable devices often relies on raw signal readings that change significantly due to calibration variations in equipment, affecting the generalizability of models. To address this challenge, developers typically adjust data on a large scale, but this approach may not be feasible for small-scale projects, like student research projects. Furthermore, it tends to overlook the benefits of federated learning in activity recognition, where a server can easily adjust models to accommodate calibration differences. In this paper, we present FedHealth, a novel approach that enables a server and client devices to jointly develop and apply models to address calibration issues in wearable devices without exchanging raw data. We conducted experiments on wearable activity recognition using a ring accelerometer and found that FedHealth enhanced the accuracy of models by 26% compared to traditional methods and 14% compared to static federated learning. Additionally, our findings revealed that FedHealth exhibited robust performance in handling various calibration issues, such as axis misalignment and signal amplitude fluctuations. Our research demonstrated the effectiveness of FedHealth in accurately predicting activities on wearable devices with calibration variations, offering a viable solution for small-scale, low-resource settings. Our code is available at https://github.com/yongchen20/FedHealth. We also provide sample datasets and instructions on how to use them at https://fedhealth.ai/. We look forward to collaborating with the research community to explore additional applications of FedHealth. This process is significantly complicated by the numerous possible ways to form a panel for each job, making traditional optimization methods inefficient due to excessive computational requirements. The study also delves into possible panel assembly strategies, examines factors that influence them, and presents an empirical analysis of the current state of algorithmic solutions in recruitment tasks. Combining the influence of modeling errors and noise in PTA data, we determine the accuracy of approximate solutions in different applications. For a fractal model, we find that the approximate solutions offer comparable precision to other approaches used for PTA data analyses. The resulting analysis involves a system of non-linear PDEs, specifically a combination of the Heisenberg ferromagnetic XY model and the KP equation, whose solutions allow us to determine the velocity distribution of the second-class particle for all time. The relationship between the system's initial conditions and the velocity distribution can be examined through the use of integrable hierarchies and the method of inverse scattering. The study also includes an examination of the associated system of non-linear PDEs in the stationary case, where we find that the resulting system corresponds to the Ginzburg-Landau equation in one spatial dimension. The integration of the system in the stationary case is accompanied by an explicit computation of the correlation function of the XY model. A key challenge in DNA data storage systems arises from the limited precision of DNA sequence readings, which leads to difficulties in retrieving digital data. To address this issue, researchers have proposed various methods for enhancing read accuracy, including the use of primer pairs to decode multiple stored bits with a single polymerase chain reaction process. However, the storage capacity managed by these decoding methods remains underutilized due to the requirement for substantial storage space for decoding ensembles. To overcome this limitation, a novel approach has been developed that leverages primer pairs with variable lengths to decode differentiable bits without compromising read accuracy. This approach, in turn, enables the development of an algorithm that strategically encodes data to minimize storage capacity and efficiently manage storage partitions. As a result, this approach can decode $n$ bits from $\lfloor2n+1\rfloor$ base pairs, outperforming the current best practice of decoding $2n$ bits from $4n$ base pairs by a significant margin of $125\%$ while reducing storage capacity by $33.3\%$. As an added benefit, this research reveals that varying primer pair lengths can be used to implement error-correcting codes, leading to a significant improvement in read accuracy and a decrease in required storage capacity. Accurate riverbed bathymetry estimation is crucial for understanding the dynamics of rivers, particularly during flooding.  A new geostatistical approach called Principal Component Generalized Anomaly (PCGA) has been developed to efficiently combine flow velocity measurements with spatial prior information for bathymetry estimation.  This PCGA model specifically utilizes the leading spatial patterns of variations to enhance geostatistical predictions, resulting in a method for bathymetry estimation called PCGA Depth (PCGAd).  A comprehensive numerical experiment was conducted to evaluate PCGAd, and the results showed that PCGAd outperformed the original CGA method, especially when prior information was available.  A real-world application of PCGAd was demonstrated through the analysis of a river with complex bathymetry features near Vicksburg, Mississippi, where additional prior information was incorporated to improve the PCGAd results.  Overall, PCGAd proved to be an effective tool for combining flow velocity measurements and prior information for riverbed bathymetry estimation, and it has significant potential for use in dynamic river environments.  A software package is available for public use to facilitate future PCGAd applications. These fusion images are often shared online, and the massive amount of data enables machine learning to improve image processing.  Currently available methods that automatically produce high dynamic range images rely on deep learning models and typically use image quality assessment techniques. The resulting insights reveal how initial conditions' heterogeneity and changing connectivity patterns influence the rate of diffusion. The study's key findings counterintuitively suggest that increased correlations actually slow the diffusion rate, whereas variations among the population accelerate it. The proposed model is contrasted with four alternative explanations for innovation adoption, including the technology adoption curve, before demonstrating its versatility by adapting the standard cumulative distribution function. The implications of our research on the dynamics of spread are far-reaching and offer a foundation for extending the model to more complex and interconnected systems. The inherent simplicity and Gaussian nature of the proposed model provide a durable platform for exploring the intricate dynamics of spread and heterogeneity, even in the presence of correlations. Process conformance checking aims to verify that observed data adheres to a presumed process model. Most existing methods check the consistency of process models with event streams over fixed time periods. In contrast, our novel approach, called Decentralized Conformance Checking for Streams (DECCS), assesses the conformance of event streams to a process model with temporal tags, even in decentralized scenarios. A key concept in our method is the Distributed Concept Graph (DCG), which for each event stream pair facilitates the computation of a more precise temporal relationship, already accounted for in DECCS. Consequently, the extension of DCG to multiple process models and event streams is the natural next step, which we refer to as Distributed Concept Graph (DCR). Our innovation, DCR, offers a more comprehensive understanding of process changes over time by mapping events to a structured framework. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method using artificial and real-world data. Additionally, we provide practical guidelines for implementing DECCS in centralized settings. Our research provides a foundation for further improvements in process conformance checking, even in centralized scenarios. Our code is available at https://github.com/SebastianVega/DECCS. Our approach is applicable to process models containing sequential processes, parallel processes, and loop processes, as demonstrated by our experiments using real data from the healthcare industry. Our results show that our method accurately identifies temporal relationships with high precision (0.92) and low false positives rates (1.28) when comparing to golden data ranges manually defined by process experts. Instead, it yields a moduli space $M_d^{gh}$ with multiple components, and computing the Taylor series expansion allows us to remove non-singular components, similar to the process described by Allombert. Ultimately, this process results in a compactification of the manifold $M_d^{ext}$, providing a more nuanced understanding of how the non-singular components of $M_d^{ext}$ arise geometrically versus how they arise via Hodge theory. We observed a notable NUV-r color shift (>1.4) beyond z~2 in the spectra of 679 galaxies, spanning a broad mass range (10^8-10^11 dollars). The observed NUV-r color exhibited a distinct dependence on galaxy mass, displaying a marked shift for galaxies weighing more than 10^9 dollars. The (250-)r color also demonstrated a reliance on galaxy mass but with a notable shift for galaxies weighing more than 10^10 dollars. Neural machine translation has seen significant advancements in recent years, thanks in part to the widespread use of LSTMs and self-learning sequences. However, the limitations of these models become apparent when applied to tasks that require transferring knowledge across different languages. One such example is when a model trained to classify English text is used to classify text in a different language, such as Spanish. In order to overcome this limitation, we propose the Multi-Sentence Dual Attention Encoder, a proprietary LSTM architecture that effectively learns the embedded representations of single sentences. Recently, Visual Relationship Detection VRD has incorporated external knowledge to improve its accuracy, with the proposal generation network being specifically affected by incorrect negative samples in its supervision. To address this challenge, we present Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling BNPS, a method that adapts Pointwise Proposal Sampling to effectively handle negative proposals. To enhance model performance through relational knowledge, we introduce a new strategy, Relational Knowledge Guided Training RKG, which leverages both primary and secondary relations to train the model. To improve the quality of generated proposals, we propose a simple yet effective method, Balanced Proposal Sampling BPS. To evaluate our approach, we conduct extensive experiments on the VRD dataset and the MS COCO dataset, both with and without explicit object proposals, achieving superior results to current state-of-the-art methods. To support widespread adoption, we open-source our code and VRD baseline models at https://github.com/Qianhewu/VRD.

Galaxies forming for the first time are subject to gravitational influence by nearby galaxies, which can lead to the accretion of streams, affecting the galaxy's structure and preventing it from fully developing a bulge, as observed in low-redshift galaxies. To investigate this phenomenon, we used the GALAXY formation simulator to model the accretion of streams for 2000 galaxies with different masses, ages, and chemical compositions. We ran the simulator for 13 billion years, stopping at 1 billion years when galaxies like LVL 1147-0251 begin distinct bulge and disk components. Based on an analysis of the galactic stream accretion, we propose a new multi-parameter model, which we applied to the previous galaxy formation simulator to gain a deeper understanding of galaxy formation. We observed that the addition of streams accelerates the formation of both the bulge and the disk, depending on the stream's mass, movement speed, and distance from the galaxy. However, if the stream misses the galaxy by too wide a margin, it fragments into satellite galaxies instead of contributing to the main galaxy's growth. We also discovered that the distribution of galaxy components varies significantly with accretion events, which can result in the formation of multiple distinct components within a single galaxy. We found specific patterns in the chemical compositions of galaxies formed through stream accretion, which could be used as indicators of their formation history. Finally, we propose a new explanation for the relationship between galaxy mass and the formation of stellar clusters, attributing it to the effect of stream accretion rather than internal cluster disruption. If we exclude stream accretion events in our simulator, we no longer observe the established correlation between galaxy mass and cluster formation, leading us to suggest observing such patterns in real galaxies will provide a record of their formation history. We also propose a way to calculate the probability of a galaxy experiencing a particular accretion event based on its current mass, age, and chemical composition, which we demonstrated by accurately predicting the properties of galaxy VCC1211. Finally, we propose observing the distribution of elemental ratios, especially iron and silicon, which we found vary significantly with accretion events, which could be compared to our simulator in the future. The explosive spread of fake news on social media platforms is caused, in part, by the ease of generating fabricated articles that rank high in search results. Existing approaches to detecting fabricated news are primarily based on text characteristics, without considering the underlying mechanics of generation. To address this, a novel generative adversarial model called MetaFEND is proposed, which generates artificial metadata with the help of a meta-model, and uses this synthetic data to train a detection network to find fabricated news. Experimental results show that MetaFEND boosts the accuracy of fabricated news detection and highlights the artificial metadata's inherent value as a feature set. To facilitate reproducibility, the code and datasets for both real and fabricated news are made publicly available.

This paper examines a one-dimensional transport equation with periodic conditions and a nonlocal flux, where solutions starting from odd initial data without sharp edges behave differently, depending on the speed of transport. If the speed is subcritical, solutions remain smooth for an infinite period. In contrast, if the speed is supercritical, solutions will develop infinite stress at some point in time. A solution that reaches a state of infinite stress will experience a breakdown, but under the condition of no dissipation, this state is considered unstable. Consequently, the solution will break into a sequence of successively smaller shockless solitons. If the speed is transcritical, solutions starting from given initial conditions will gradually transform into a soliton with the same speed and an ongoing, infinite stress that results in a disappearing soliton. Ultimately, this soliton will shrink to a point of infinite stress with the formation of a hole, or void, which will expand over time. A key observation from numerical data reveals that this particular transport equation exhibits an unexpected preference for solutions with soliton-like characteristics. A related model, the one-dimensional inviscid Burgers equation with periodic conditions and nonlocal flux, also exhibits this soliton preference. A modification of this model, with an additional term representing a small amount of dissipation, will eventually break down due to increasing stress, but with a different outcome. Instead of the formation of a hole, it will experience a continuous decrease in the size of successively smaller shockless solitons until they eventually disappear. A similar analysis applies to a model with a fixed stress threshold. A numerical investigation of these models reveals that even those with no dissipation whatsoever will eventually experience a decrease in the size of successively smaller shockless solitons until they disappear. Researchers are leveraging quantum knowledge to create precise and sensitive mass sensors. A potential breakthrough in this field could result from using silicon quantum dots as weight-sensitive devices, thanks to their robustness in maintaining reliability through environmental changes. A possible hindrance to achieving this goal is the exchange interaction causing fluctuations in the quantum states, albeit this dependence can be finely tuned by introducing impurities. Our study delves into the effect of placed dopants on the Heisenberg spin exchange interaction within a silicon crystal lattice, revealing varying levels of exchange coupling anywhere from very weak to quite strong, spanning multiple micrometers. Notably, we discovered that exchange coupling can become extremely fragile, varying significantly in response to changes in the quantum dot volume, but remaining consistently changeable with volume modifications, thus offering a feasible adjustment capability. Ultimately, our findings suggest that exchange interaction's unpredictable nature can be reliably managed through the careful placement of dopants, a prerequisite for developing silicon-based mass sensors that are insensitive to the surrounding environment. Our approach provides a solid foundation for predicting exchange-dependent phenomena in silicon quantum dots and offers actionable guidelines for executing controlled manipulation of zero-valley states in silicon quantum dots, a level of control that is both feasible and essential for developing mass sensors with improved precision. Our research indicates that exchange-dependent zero-valley states' resilience can be significantly enhanced through the careful placement of dopants, an achievable level of control that is crucial for developing mass sensors with improved precision, as well as reliable and scalable silicon-based quantum processors. This model leverages a compact CNN to efficiently annotate regions of interest (ROIs) by transforming them into feature maps that can be used for classification and distance metric computation. To further enhance efficiency, a Convolutional Neural Network is used to approximate the popular Euclidean distance metric. This resulting model is simple, highly effective, and capable of generating precise 3D segmentations. Experimental validation utilizing clinical data from 10 patients demonstrates its superior performance when compared to conventional techniques. Furthermore, this model exhibits a significant reduction in computational demands, making it ideally suited for time-constrained, clinically-relevant applications. Deep Neural Network based features have gained significant popularity in various classification tasks and have been found to be highly accurate, surpassing conventional methods. Nonetheless, obtaining these features is challenging without the model, requiring significant computational resources. These graphs possess intricate properties, featuring infinite ranks according to their automorphism groups, a characteristic shared by only a handful of other graphs holding this ranking feat. Additionally, the m,n pairs and p,q,r singles demonstrate remarkable versatility in their structural configuration, allowing them to be modified to manifest specific symmetric properties, thereby expanding the already substantial repertoire of symmetric graphs beyond the current recorded count. Furthermore, our discovery reveals that the vast majority of cubic graphs with symmetric properties are actually members of the m,n pairs or p,q,r singles, a finding revealed through our in-depth analysis of 575 such cubic graphs, an exhaustive sample comprising every possible case of planar embedded cubic graph with a specific set of symmetry features. Lastly, our work also uncovers intriguing connections between the concept of a rational distance and a particular type of polynomial equation, thereby establishing a novel link between graph theory and number theory. In related research, we have successfully classified all infinite chains of singles that are composed of an infinite sequence of consecutive rational distances, an achievement we had initially struggled to accomplish. The Group Lasso method, as proposed by Lagrange, Lin, and Wright in 2009, allows for the elimination of entire groups of variables from linear models by setting their coefficients to zero. We have adapted this technique for use in logistic regression models, even with continuous and categorical input data. This has been made possible through the application of natural groupings of categorical variables, based on their interpretation in regression analysis. A novel algorithm has been developed to solve for model coefficients and perform variable selection via the Group Lasso method. This algorithm produces a sparse solution, and its efficiency has been demonstrated through the inclusion of multiple features in linear models. When tested on both simulated and real-world datasets, it has shown superior performance, in comparison to existing methods, in terms of mean squared error and classification accuracy. A key advantage of this method is the automatic selection of relevant categorical variables and their interactions in regression models. In addition to its variability selection capabilities, the algorithm has the potential to enhance the interpretability of models, particularly in scenarios with multiple categorical variables. This research has been an invitation to explore the Group Lasso method in conjunction with other techniques, such as graph-based methods, for variable selection in machine learning. A novel speech enhancement model is proposed, dubbed Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN), combining Convolution Recurrent Networks with spectral masks to achieve better performance in the time-frequency domain.  DPCRN consists of three primary components that work in tandem to produce improved frequency spectra: the T-DNN block refines the speech spectrum, the DPCN block eliminates background noise, and the CRN block ensures that generated spectra match the statistics of the clean spectra.  To further enhance performance, DPCRN incorporates an external enhancement network that can be chosen from three alternatives: a basic enhancement network, a DPCN-based enhancement network, or a vectorized enhancement network.  Experiments conducted on the VoiceBank-DECTALK corpus using the DPCRN approach with vectorized enhancement networks achieved an objective evaluation score of 0.7927 in SDR, surpassing the current state-of-the-art speech enhancement methods.  Additionally, evaluations conducted on the MUSAN and VoiceSSH datasets yielded outstanding results in both objective and subjective evaluations.  A major advantage of DPCRN lies in its capability to effectively handle non-stationary speech and background noise.  The source code for DPCRN has been made publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/yangzw123/DPCRN. Social media sentiment analysis is a developing field of natural language processing, where machine learning models are used to assess the emotions and opinions conveyed within social media content. This study leverages a long short-term memory (LSTM) model to classify the sentiment of individual Twitter tweets. By using a binary sentiment classification framework, we demonstrated that LSTMs can effectively determine the positive or negative nature of a tweet. This achievement served as a foundation for an in-depth examination of how to enhance sentiment classification accuracy through the aggregation of multiple Twitter opinions sharing common hashtags. This is a relevant issue in today's social media age, where many individuals engage in online discussions and express their opinions on various topics. When evaluating public policies or commercial products, researchers often need to assess the sentiment of Twitter discussions related to those topics. However, considering the rapid pace at which new tweets are posted, there is a significant challenge in relying solely on manual sentiment assessments. This issue can be addressed by developing and testing machine learning models on large datasets, which requires substantial computational resources and numerous positively labeled samples to train the models effectively. This research demonstrated that LSTMs can be highly efficient in this context, as they yielded a 90% accuracy rate in classifying the sentiment of individual Twitter tweets. Moreover, by integrating the aggregated opinions shared under the same hashtag, we achieved a precision of 90.7% in classifying multiple Twitter opinions as positive or negative. This precision rate ranged from 84.1% to 98.1% for different datasets, which further validated the effectiveness of using LSTMs in this application. This study's findings provide a solid foundation for the development of machine learning models that can efficiently handle large-scale Twitter sentiment classification tasks, which is highly valuable for researchers and policymakers who often engage with such data sets. This research is particularly relevant to areas like public policy evaluation, financial forecasting, and commercial market analysis, which heavily rely on Twitter sentiment analysis. This is the first study that explores the integration of machine learning models and social network analysis in the context of Twitter sentiment classification, which offers novel and exciting possibilities for combining both natural and social data attributes to enhance classification accuracy. We develop a method for examining the evolution of optical tomograms, focusing on how their nonclassical characteristics, such as entanglement, transform over time. To demonstrate this approach, we apply it to a diverse selection of optical states in a two-mode scenario: Bell states, number states, and coherent states, and observe the progression of their entanglement dynamics. Furthermore, we investigate the effects of photon loss on these states and measure the remaining entanglement as quantified by the concurrence, finding that it adheres to a particular decay pattern. If the initial state has a specific mean photon number, the entanglement dynamics exhibits a double-exponential decay pattern, supported by a mathematical proof. If the mean photon number is unknown, we determine an alternative parameterization based on the optical tomogram itself, which also reveals a double-exponential character. Ultimately, this investigation highlights the significance of considering the dynamics of nonclassical effects in open systems, and suggests possible applications in estimating lost entanglement. To facilitate this research, we develop an intuitive graphical representation of entanglement dynamics in the multi-mode scenario. If the number of modes exceeds two, we propose an alternative measure of entanglement, the reduced density matrix's trace, which we find retains a double-exponential decay pattern in the face of photon loss. This investigation is an initial step towards assessing the recoverability of lost entanglement from optical tomograms in open systems. To achieve this goal, we propose several possible revival windows based on the mean photon number, which could be utilized to enhance the efficiency of entanglement purification protocols. Finally, we analyze the effectiveness of two distinct purification methods: the Karhunen-Loé algorithm combined with the action of a beam splitter, and a genetic algorithm implemented through a binary mask, finding that the latter is more efficient in recovering lost entanglement for certain initial conditions. This research paves the way for developing strategies to revive lost nonclassical effects in open systems, and demonstrates the value of examining the entanglement dynamics in the optical tomogram representation. Immersive video navigation can be enhanced through viewport prediction, which anticipates the viewer's interest region based on visual and audio cues. Video subtitles have significant potential to enhance prediction performance due to their widespread inclusion in online videos. In this study, a novel approach is introduced that leverages video subtitles in addition to standard features for viewport prediction in an immersive video navigation framework. In order to accommodate subtitles, the approach modifies viewer interaction data, resulting in a more precise viewport prediction model. Experimental evaluations conducted on extensive datasets demonstrate the proposed approach's superiority over the baseline model, with significant accuracy improvements of 26.1% and 12.9% in the VYP and VYP-LT assessment metrics, respectively. Additionally, the study provides insights into effective subtitle-based viewport prediction through the visualization of predicted vs. actual viewports and viewer interaction heatmaps. Furthermore, the proposed approach is found to perform better for videos with more precise viewports and those featuring multiple relevant objects. The study's findings highlight the substantial impact of video subtitles on viewer interaction and presents a viable solution for predicting viewer interest regions in immersive video content. The proposed subtitle-based viewport prediction approach is viable for extensive applications in emerging immersive technologies. These codes enable us to approximate both thermal states and time-evolved systems, with a level of precision determined by a bond dimension that scales asymptotically like the square root of the system size, irrespective of its logarithm. This development offers a promising platform for verifying the efficacy of approximate, large-scale quantum simulations. We also demonstrate the applicability and efficiency of these constructions for approximating both random pure state preparations and Coherent Quantum Classically Coherent circuits. Moreover, our findings imply that there are asymptotically scalable solutions for approximating both uniform mixture states and time-evolved versions of an arbitrary quantum circuit, with a bond dimension that scales polynomially in comparison to the number of qubits. We further illustrate the practical advantages of these constructions by conducting a quantum simulation of approximately solving a random instances of the Lipschitz Maximization Problem using both a classical simulation for small-scale systems and a quantum simulation for larger-scale systems. Both simulations employ the same metropolitan explorer agent-based model, yet the quantum simulation employs a reduced bond dimension that scales polynomially with the number of agents, indicating a significant improvement over prior approaches where the required bond dimension increased exponentially with the number of qubits. Knowledge distillation is a significant technique for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a complex one. The traditional method requires access to the original network's output, but black-box settings are more practical, where only the input and corresponding labels are available. We introduce decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, a novel approach that uses classification decisions from the compressed model to teach a more compact one, differentiating it from existing methods that rely on soft labels. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by training mobile neural networks for MNIST, Fashion MNIST, and EMNIST datasets, achieving a significant compression ratio improvement without sacrificing accuracy. Our method showcases particular advantages in extremely compact models, outperforming state-of-the-art methods according to the assessment metric used. Quantum information flow between an open system and its surroundings can proceed in both directions, resulting in both energy transfer and signal transmission. To illustrate this concept, a simple quantum system consisting of a single qubit is connected to a one-qubit environment also representing noise. Through a joint unitary operation, both information loss to the environment and a signal transmitted to a separate one-qubit target can be achieved. This effect is susceptible to noise and requires both a specific initial qubit state and an appropriately tailored target qubit. As both the system and target qubits are separated, this example demonstrates inter-convertible information and signal transmission between an open system and its environment in a quantum context, thereby illustrating the idea of bidirectional information flow. Additionally, this example can serve as a precursor to addressing information retention in the presence of noise. Furthermore, it showcases the convertibility of heat and qubit number in specific initial states. Ultimately, this example has implications for quantum thermodynamics, in particular, in relation to the extractable work from a target qubit as heat has been generated in the environment. It also paves the way for investigating the remaining information in the system and environment. It is worth noting that both the system and target qubits are unconnected and the information transmitted to the target qubit cannot be reversed. This example is an extension of previous research on unidirectional information flow. It is also an extension of previous work on qubit number and heat convertibility in specific initial states, encompassing both coherent and incoherent conditions.
