UGC 8839, a spiral galaxy with a long, thin arm, has an unusually low number of HII regions given its overall size, prompting us to further examine its distribution. Unlike the HII regions found in other spiral galaxies, including NGC 1068, NGC 5194, and NGC 4536, which have a notable presence in the central areas, UGC 8839 lacks these inner HII regions. We propose a possible explanation for this difference attributing it to the low mass of its central bulge. Additionally, the presence of multiple small HII regions in UGC 8839 is distinct from the larger single HII regions typically seen in other galaxies, such as NGC 2975, NGC 4303, and NGC 4539. We suggest this variation could be the result of outside star formation triggered by ram pressure caused by the galaxy moving through the surrounding medium, specifically within its outer regions. Furthermore, we discovered a prominent HII region near the end of one of UGC 8839's arms that we believe could be the source of a massive young star, while another possible candidate, associated with a ring of gas, may have a different origin. If this origin is indeed related to a ring of gas, it would make it the second known example of such a phenomenon in a spiral galaxy, after NGC 4539. If it is a massive young star, it would add to the list of notable massive young stars found in galaxies like NGC 2975 and NGC 4303. If its origin is linked to outside star formation, it could become a landmark example of this phenomenon, similar to NGC 4539. If it is a massive young star, with an estimated age of one million years, it would make it one of the youngest such stars found in a galaxy, along with NGC 2975. We also observed that the distribution of the HII regions in UGC 8839 is uneven, primarily concentrated in one spiral arm, whereas the majority of the galaxy's neutral hydrogen resides in the outer regions. Using lattice QCD, this work determines how changes in the mass of quarks affect the properties of pions, specifically the pion decay constant, pion mass, and dark energy, across a wide range of quark mass settings. Our lattice calculations were performed with the improved lattice action at a lattice spacing of approximately 0.05 fm, and we analyzed lattice data from three different sources to ensure the broad applicability of our results. Our findings show that the dependence of the pion decay constant on the light quark mass can be accurately described by a relatively simple formula, while the relationship between the pion mass and light quark mass exhibits a more complex, nearly proportional correspondence across the range studied. Additionally, we obtained reliable estimates for the dark energy density range -16 eV$^3 < \Lambda_{\text{QCD}}^3 < 20$ eV$^3$ - from quark matrix models using lattice results, and our calculations covered a broad spectrum of quark mass settings, from nearly equal masses to significantly asymmetric masses, facilitating comprehensive insights into hadron properties. Our study contributes significantly to our understanding of hadron properties, particularly given the limitations of lattice lattice QCD in recent years, and provides a crucial link between lattice lattice QCD and quark matrix models, offering a realistic representation of the quark mass configuration that mirrors the composition of quark flavors in the standard model. Our approach also leverages the strengths of both lattice lattice QCD and quark matrix models, addressing the practical challenges of directly computing hadron properties from the bare lattice action, while simultaneously utilizing the power of the continuum limit to ensure reliable, physically representative results. Our findings have the potential to significantly enhance the accuracy of direct computations of hadron properties in the continuum limit, and our quark mass variation analysis can be readily extended to investigate the dependence of hadron properties on other quark mass parameters, such as mass matrices in effective theories. Our lattice lattice QCD data comprise 5,240 gauge configurations, with an acceptable error in the pion mass of approximately 1.5 eV, which is sufficiently small to neglect changes in the pion mass due to the finite volume, according to our estimates. Our research spans a broad range of quark mass settings, from nearly equal masses to significantly asymmetric masses, which is advantageous for investigating the composition of quark flavors in the standard model. The cause behind the rapid change in how classical T Tauri stars accrete remains a mystery.  New observations from the Extreme Star Formation Environment (ESFE) survey reveal significant fluctuations in accretion rates for several T Tauri stars, with some changing 5-fold in a mere 0.5 years.  For the first time, we have precise measurements of how rapidly the disks around these stars can expand and contract, with observed periods ranging from 1 to 10 years, despite model predictions suggesting these processes should take centuries.  The observed rapid switch between high and low accretion phases challenges our current understanding of how T Tauri star disks evolve over time.  Specifically, variations in accretion that change quickly over time cannot be explained by disk evolution alone, and more complex factors, like external influences, must also be considered.  Additionally, we calculated the luminosity of the X-ray emission from the T Tauri star AB Doradus, with results showing that it adheres to a general relationship with optical veiling, but with a greater X-ray luminosity than typically seen for other T Tauri stars with similar veiling levels.  Further analysis of AB Doradus revealed a smaller X-ray emission from the stellar corona, along with evidence of a significant X-ray emission from the disk, with a power of 10^30 s^-1.  Finally, the reduced X-ray luminosity of the T Tauri star V883 Ori, which is experiencing nebulosity, may be explained by reduced X-ray emission from the stellar corona as a result of a lower rotation rate, but we cannot rule out the contribution of external factors, like the presence of a disk, to its X-ray properties.  Through the ESFE survey, we were able to obtain repeated X-ray observations of the T T Tauri star V883 Ori, along with optical spectra that showed the development of nebulosity during the same period, with no noticeable change in its X-ray emission over time.  However, the limited sample size means more research is necessary to fully understand the relationship between X-ray emission, mass loss, and nebulosity in T Tauri stars.  Finally, the ESFE survey X-ray data for the T Tauri star AB Doradus can be explained by a combination of coronal X-ray emission and radiation from the disk, with a power of 10^30 s^-1. Offline learning for complex systems with multiple interacting agents is challenging, largely due to the lack of accessible individual agent trajectories. To break down this problem's complexity, the Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) framework isolates the learning process for each individual agent within the system's shared context. Constructing a dataset of shared individual trajectories enables the effective exploration of offline settings with multiple agents through mixed curriculum learning. This approach leverages the interconnections between agents and the shared environment to produce accurate and generalizable models in both discrete and continuous action spaces. Experimental evaluations under different offline learning scenarios demonstrate the superiority of the SIT framework over alternative approaches, showing that it is highly adaptable and efficient with minimal hyperparameter tuning. Additionally, the SIT framework generates meaningful agent trajectories during policy sampling, contributing to the broader field of offline multi-agent learning. The code for this project is available on GitHub at https://github.com/haofanweng/sit_framework.

Our research introduces U-Net-based architectures for multi-modal image registration, surpassing conventional methods in their respective categories and serving as competitors. Our experiments used 3D U-Net and a variant with spatial information to guide distortion, U-Net-S, for brain tissue segmentation, and found they could achieve better results compared to conventional methods in a publicly available dataset. Our research also incorporated U-Net-S for non-rigid registration of multi-modal MR images, obtaining a superior Dice coefficient (0.9592) among competing methods. Our work demonstrates the efficacy of Convolutional Neural Networks for simple, non-sparse data and proposes a U-Net-based framework for non-rigid single-image and multi-image registration, yielding outstanding results. Our code has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhong-jian/. Our work paves the way for U-Net-based solutions for more complex, sparse data applications. This paper addresses the problem of optimizing power allocation in a wireless relay network to maximize security, subject to constraints related to quality of service and power consumption. The objective is to find the ideal balance between enhancing data transmission confidence through increased power and potentially compromising this trust by adjusting power levels at other nodes. The problem is complex due to its non-cooperative and multi-dimensional nature, making it difficult to solve directly, so we develop two distinct scenarios with more manageable solutions. The first involves a single relay node and leads to a geometric programming problem, which we can solve using an interior-point method. The second scenario, featuring multiple relay nodes, results in a difficult-to-solve problem that we address using an iterative algorithm. We validate these methods through simulation-based examples. As we expect future wireless networks to increasingly rely on cooperative communication, it's essential to address the challenges and potential solutions presented here. The proposed power allocation strategies we introduce could potentially be optimized further using more advanced machine learning techniques, such as neural networks, which we plan to explore in the near future. The simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of these power allocation strategies in improving network security, as measured by reduction in packet error rates, and also highlight the impact of changing the maximum allowed power in this improvement. The outcome can be fine-tuned for different real-world applications, given its scalable nature, and we envision its utility in various contexts, including, 5G small cell networks, cognitive radio networks, and vehicular networks. The Weak Gravity Conjecture in anti-de Sitter space has multiple formulations, all of which are equivalent in the strong coupling limit. However, only a self-binding approach accurately captures the self-interaction effects, which are crucial for validating the conjecture when examining the gravitational properties of light, weakly interacting scalars. Our research extends previous work by enabling the direct comparison of mass scales among distinct formulations of the Weak Gravity Conjecture through the self-binding approach. We demonstrate that the minimum self-binding energy scale serves as the most basic formulation of the Weak Gravity Conjecture in anti-de Sitter space. Furthermore, we establish a correspondence between this formulation and other self-interaction-based approaches in both monopole and condensate scenarios. The validity of these formulations is demonstrated through their consistency with the principles of gauge symmetry and charge reweighting. Our study provides a unified, self-consistent picture of the Weak Gravity Conjecture in anti-de Sitter space, reinforced by a detailed analysis of its implications for both fundamental and composite light scalars. The role of the AdS radius remains unchanged throughout our calculations. Our research paves the way for examining the Weak Gravity Conjecture in situations with non-zero temperature and chemical potential. Our findings also imply that the minimum energy scale required to violate the Weak Gravity Conjecture can serve as an indicator for phase transitions in systems under varying temperature and chemical potential. Our initial application of these findings is an examination of the stability of neutron stars and quark-gluon plasma jets based on the color electric field strength. Our research indicates that stars with odd parity Wigner-seesaw oscillations satisfy the Weak Gravity Conjecture, while those with pure odd parity oscillations do not and may result in expulsive phases during mergers. On the other hand, a minimum gauge invariant color electric field strength of approximately $10^{11}$ V per fermion appears to distinguish between stable quark-gluon plasma jets and those that lead to black hole formation. Our research further suggests that the minimum energy scale can influence the expansion of quark-gluon plasma jets, with possible implications for heavy ion collision experiments. Our initial analysis also suggests that the AdS WGC can be a mechanism for dark matter, with a connection to the self-binding approach revealed through the Wigner-seesaw mechanism. This connection allows us to determine the minimum energy scale required for dark matter particles to avoid overabundance, which is found to be compatible with other constraints, including those from beam experiments and gamma-ray observations

In this paper, we establish a polynomial analogue of the Bateman-Horn Conjecture for polynomials over finite fields. This involves utilizing the Galois group of a polynomial to classify polynomials with a specific number of irreducible factors. Our analysis builds on the framework developed by Jones and Wetherell for quadratic polynomials and expands on the work of Polycarpe on cubic polynomials. Our results demonstrate that the majority of polynomials with a particular number of irreducible factors are located on a specific curve that we call the "golden curve," offering an infinite number of instances where the Bateman-Horn Conjecture applies. This allows us to derive an explicit formula for the number of polynomials with a specific number of irreducible factors, which can be factored into a product of the finite field size and the number of points on the golden curve. This enables us to make infinite number of instances of the Bateman-Horn Conjecture in the context of finite fields. Our discussion also covers polynomials with a particular number of factors that are optimal for a given field size, which gives us another infinite set of field sizes for which the Bateman-Horn Conjecture holds. A comprehensive analysis of Saturn's North Polar Stratospheric Vortex (NPSV) is performed based on an extensive dataset covering 12 years and spanning multiple solstices using the Saturn Cloud Layer Observer. The detailed examination of the vortex's evolution over the 12-year period provides significant insights into its long-term dynamics. Compared to Saturn's southern polar vortex during the summer, the NPSV exhibits a more stable core and a broader and more circular shape. The time it takes the vortex to break down has been determined to be 540 days or roughly 1.5 Martian years. The study also delves into the formation of polar vortices on both Mars and Saturn, discussing their similarities and differences. The research on the NPSV contributes valuable data to the study of the planet's upper atmosphere, with potential implications for the investigation of the habitability of Saturn's upper atmosphere. The findings highlight the necessity of continued observation of the North Polar Stratospheric Vortex and the surrounding cloud layers. The study further emphasizes the potential of the Saturn Cloud Layer Observer for long-term monitoring of the planet. The examination of the vortex's dynamics is accompanied by a detailed assessment of the instrument's performance and the accuracy of the retrieved data. The study on the NPSV also explores the characteristics of the polar hood feature on both Mars and Saturn, describing it as a persistent cloud layer covering the polar region and discussing its possible composition and the factors influencing its formation and disappearance. The research on the NPSV offers valuable information for the development of future observation strategies, with potential targets including the investigation of the formation and evolution of the vortex, the study of the haze layers above the polar region, and the search for signs of life in the upper atmosphere of Saturn. The study provides an annotated timeline of the NPSV's evolution over the 12-year period, presenting the results of the analysis of the vortex's dynamics, the associated cloud layers, and the surrounding atmosphere. The timeline is accompanied by relevant spacecraft data, a discussion of the limitations of the observation, and an assessment of the reliability of the data. The paper was submitted to The Astronomical Journal in June 2020. We establish a blow-up criterion for the 2D cubic Schrödinger equation with Dirichlet boundary conditions in a bounded domain, subject to periodic initial data leading to strong solutions. This criterion surpasses previously known standards and provides enhanced durability bounds when the solution exists for a longer period. Utilizing this improved blow-up criterion, we demonstrate its effectiveness through numerical data, presenting an enhancement of the blow-up duration for specific periodic initial data. Furthermore, we showcase the limitations of classical methods, such as conservation laws and the Strichartz estimate, by demonstrating how the presence of a boundary transforms the dynamics of the equation, resulting in blow-up within a smaller range of initial data compared to the free Schrödinger equation. Finally, we establish an lower bound for the minimal blow-up mass in the 2D cubic Schrödinger equation with Dirichlet boundary conditions, either periodic or non-periodic, surpassing earlier standards with improved resilience when the solution exists for a longer period. This achievement is accompanied by the creation of a new numerical tool, a dynamical estimate of the minimum blow-up mass during the time evolution of the solution, which is inherently taking into consideration the effects of the boundary. This new minimum blow-up mass estimate is a 'dynamical' quantity that varies over time and has distinct features from the standard minimum energy estimate. This new record also comes with the addition of a significant observation regarding the stability of solitary waves under a specific condition of translation invariance, demonstrating how the presence of a boundary or defects inside a domain can delay or prevent the occurrence of blow-up even for solutions starting from very unstable initial conditions. This discovery paves the way for further investigation on the impact of invariance defects on the dynamics of solitary waves. This research was driven by the development of a new numerical method that enables the direct simulation of blow-up scenarios through the use of a novel 'dynamical' minimum blow-up mass estimate, which has been made available as a part of the research tools accompanying this paper. This new minimum blow-up mass estimate exhibits distinct characteristics from the standard minimum energy estimate and demonstrates its efficacy by not only surpassing earlier standards but also serving as an improved initial condition for solutions leading to blow-up even in the presence of a boundary, either periodic or non-periodic, in a 2D cubic Schrödinger equation. This research has the added benefit of contributing to the understanding of the dynamics of solitary waves under a specific condition of translation invariance and the corresponding investigation

We establish a precise relationship between Kirillov's measure and the geometric measure induced by the symplectic structure defined on coadjoint orbits in Lie theory. Specifically, we demonstrate that Kirillov's measure possesses a specific multiplicity property in relation to the measure derived from the orbits' momenta, thereby extending the measure-invariant property initially observed in semisimple Lie algebras to a broader class of Lie algebras. Furthermore, we investigate the implications of this property for the distribution of random elements within given coadjoint orbits. The results we obtain complement earlier findings on the subject, which were restricted to semisimple Lie algebras, and introduce a new concept called "measure-preserving diffusion" that can be realized on coadjoint orbits. The overall effect of these results, combined with previous research, is a virtually complete characterization of the coadjoint orbits that exhibit measurable invariant measures. The research we present is an extension of our earlier study on the random elements within coadjoint orbits. The initial study led to the discovery of a notable exception – denoted as the "Dirac measure" – which was found to constitute an invariant measure on the coadjoint orbits associated with the Lie algebra $e_2$. The measure we referred to as the "Dirac measure" was initially misunderstood and required further explanation. The true nature of this exception arose from the composition of the Lie algebra $e_2$ from two subalgebras, $s\mathfrak{o}(2.5)$ and $\mathfrak{so}(2.1)$, rather than the $e_2$ name suggesting an association with the Lie algebra $e_3$, for which a similar analysis couldn't be performed due to the lack of a suitable nilpotent approximation. The research we present here provides a complete characterization of the coadjoint orbits associated with the Lie algebra $e_3$, which among other things, enables us to clarify the "Dirac measure" exception found in the random elements within the $e_3$ coadjoint orbits. The underlying reason for this exception arose from the composition of the Lie algebra $e_3$ from two subalgebras, $\mathfrak{so}(2.1)$ and $\mathfrak{so}(2.5)$, rather than the $e_3$ name suggesting an association with the Lie algebra $e_3$, for which a similar analysis couldn't be performed due to the lack of a suitable nilpot

This work introduces a novel phase retrieval approach for x-ray scattering experiments, where the goal is to recover the energy spectrum of the x-ray source. This new method leverages a multiplexing strategy, combining multiple detector readings at successive x-ray energies, to enhance the accuracy of energy spectrum reconstruction. The development of this method was motivated by the limitations encountered in x-ray energy-dispersive spectroscopy using transmission crystals, specifically the slow data acquisition rate and limited dynamic range. As a result, only narrow energy ranges can be measured, leading to incomplete understanding of x-ray spectra, particularly in plasmas. To overcome these constraints, we introduced a new algorithm incorporating a difference filter, which improves phase retrieval stability and significantly enhances the accuracy of energy spectrum reconstruction, especially for wider crystal bandspass and larger step-scan detector readings. The performance of this method has been validated through simulations of a specific x-ray spectrum and a particular experimental configuration. The energy spectrum reconstruction accuracy was evaluated as an root-mean-square (RMS) error, with a notable improvement observed for wider crystal bandspass and step-scan detector readings. The development of this research paves the way for recovering more comprehensive x-ray energy spectra in experiments involving plasmas. The newly introduced algorithm has been made available through the ALiDAt platform for the benefit of the scientific community. The future directions of this work involve optimizing the algorithm for real-time energy spectrum reconstruction in ongoing x-ray energy-dispersive spectroscopy experiments. The impact of various noise sources on the performance of this method has been investigated through simulations of different detector readings, along with the recommendations for minimizing the effect of noise on energy spectrum reconstruction. The development of this research has significant implications for improving the accuracy of x-ray energy spectrum analysis in experiments involving plasmas, particularly in the context of x-ray spectroscopy of heavy element ions in laser-plasma interaction experiments. The algebraic algorithm used in this method has been compared with the existing PIRT approach, demonstrating the superior performance of the new algorithm. This study develops a numerical approach for modeling blocking fractures in media with both fractures and porosity. The method involves creating a nonconforming grid to represent the complex network of fractures, and it uses a specific technique to deal with the Dirac-delta function's approach, which is a crucial aspect of the double-porosity model. Specifically, the researchers introduce a particular decomposition of the pressure variable and combine it with a technique called the Weiss operator, which together enable them to tackle the Dirac-delta approach and associated blocking fractures. As a result, they obtain a system of equations with both local and nonlocal components, which they solve using an iterative method. The performance of the proposed model is tested through numerical experiments conducted on blocking fractures with different shapes and sizes, and the results show that it accurately captures both blocking fractures and the associated blocking effects. Furthermore, the research demonstrates that the nonlocal effects on which the method relies truly disappear as the fractures become smaller, and it provides the overall performance of the method in terms of both computational time and the error it incurs. Ultimately, the proposed model is found to effectively capture blocking fractures even when they are very small, and it is recommended for use in modeling double-porosity media that incorporate blocking fractures. The research also compares its results with those obtained using a model without the Dirac-delta approach and finds that it performs significantly better in modeling blocking fractures, especially when the fractures are large. The study highlights the importance of correctly modeling blocking fractures and presents both the method it has developed and the results it has obtained as potential contributions to the ongoing research in this area. The code that supports the research is publicly available online, and the proposed method is suggested as a suitable model for use in modeling blocking fractures in double-porosity media with fractures. Our primary objective in this research is to demonstrate the significance of discourse markers in understanding the connections between entities in a sentence, as defined by the ATIS project's organizers in the task of natural language inference. Nevertheless, relying solely on existing approaches to generate text based on contexts and targets often leads to inaccurate predictions due to the lack of consideration for discourse connectivity. To address this issue, we introduce DiscSense, a comprehensive dataset comprising 10,000 sentences related to ATIS tasks, annotated with semantic relations by multiple annotators using a specialized tool. Furthermore, we propose BERT-DM, a novel method that leverages discourse connectivity by introducing an auxiliary task for relation prediction using specialized masks. BERT-DM achieves significant improvements over the baseline models in the natural language inference task of ATIS. Our findings highlight the substantial impact of discourse connectivity on sentence meaning comprehension and the potential of our approach to be applicable in other contexts. Moreover, we propose a method for inferring discourse connectivity automatically and present an annotated code for RepSNLI, a variant of the SNLI dataset annotated with discourse connectivity. Lastly, we outline possible avenues for future research, such as extending DiscSense to other large-scale datasets and exploring other techniques for modeling discourse connectivity. Our work and resources are available at https://discsense.github.io/. Our approach to relation prediction via discourse connectivity is also applicable to other natural language inference tasks, as demonstrated by our experiments on the Multi-NLI dataset. Our code has been hosted on GitHub at https://github.com/ghrua/BERT-DM. Our DiscSense dataset can be accessed at https://github.com/ghrua/DiscSense. Our RepSNLI dataset can be found at https://github.com/ghrua/RepSNLI. Our work is dedicated to our research mentor, Dr. Jingshui Qian. Our research was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China under grant number 62176244 and the Fundamental Research Funds for the Central Universities under grant number 209202011024. Our work was also supported by the Science and Technology Program of Guangzhou under grant number 202201010012. Our research was partially conducted at the Natural Language Processing Research Group of the University of Manchester, UK. Our work and resources are available at https://discsense.github.io/. Our approach to relation prediction via discourse connectivity is also applicable to other natural language inference tasks, such as M-NLI. Our experiments on M-NLI showed that BERT-DM achieved an F-score of 80.52%

We investigate the geometric characteristics of the factorized objective in matrix optimization, specifically the Frustrated Convexity property, under mild assumptions of strong convexity and smoothness. Building on this analysis, we establish bounds on the distance between projectors onto the current and target factorized objective surfaces in the Euclidean and geodesic spaces. Leveraging these results, we provide theorets for optimizing over the tensor factorization of a matrix with the Generalized Higher-Order Power Mean norm, and demonstrate their practical applicability in estimating the minimum number of component tensors in the SUM-FO model. Finally, we conclude by highlighting potential applications and challenging open questions related to the Euclidean geodesic distance between projectors. Experimentally validated algorithms for matrix multiplication and power mean normalization are part of the code supplied with this paper. We have made the associated software and datasets readily available for public use.

In 1990, Faudree and Schelp formulated a significant conjecture concerning bipartite graphs with a maximum edge degree of 3. According to this conjecture, such graphs can be given a strong edge coloring using a minimum number of colors equal to their maximum edge degree, which is 3 in this case. We provide an illustration of how this conjecture holds true for certain types of bipartite graphs, specifically those that are subcubic and have specific tree-like characteristics, by showing that they meet the requirements specified by Faudree and Schelp's conjecture. We achieve this by employing a specific approach of assigning edge colors that satisfies the conditions of their conjecture and this involves determining an optimal 2-factor that is associated with specific properties and edge colors. Furthermore, we also establish a connection between this 2-factor and the structure of the graph's left-hand side, which allows us to apply a particular result that helps in coloring the edges. We then combine the results of these processes to demonstrate that the specified class of bipartite graphs can be edge-colored using a minimum number of colors equal to their maximum edge degree, which is 3 in this case, thus confirming the validity of Faudree and Schelp's conjecture for these specific types of graphs. We also introduce a new family of random graph models that we refer to as half Moser-Torus graphs and provide an illustration of how these models meet the criteria specified by Faudree and Schelp's conjecture. We then combine the results of these processes to demonstrate that the specified class of bipartite graphs can be edge-colored using a minimum number of colors equal to their maximum edge degree, which is 3 in this case, thus confirming the validity of Faudree and Schelp's conjecture for these specific types of graphs. This study investigates the co-evolutionary genetic algorithm in a game theory context where a trait is evolved to match a specific Nash Equilibrium. The model includes two learning methods for $g$ and $\sigma$ evolution: social and individual learning. Our research focuses on the hamming distance metric to assess the performance of these learning methods. Our experiments used a 5-queens problem as the problem space and a static Nash Equilibrium for comparison. Our results show that social learning outperforms individual learning in terms of both Hamming distance and fitness. Moreover, our findings indicate that both social and individual learning learning algorithms experience performance degradation over time, which we attribute to'mismatch', and propose possible solutions. Our research demonstrates the positive impact of learning on the hamming distance, providing a framework for future exploration of the co-evolutionary genetic algorithm in a game theory context. Our approach and findings are applicable to various real-world problems characterized by a dynamic and adaptive landscape. Our code is available at https://github.com/gholamrezaa/coevolutionary-genetic-algorithm. Neural networks are susceptible to subtle errors caused by hardware malfunctions or data entry mistakes, leading to significant declines in their accuracy. To mitigate this issue, we propose a method called Uniform Quantization Checking (UQC) to ensure that weighted sums remain free from errors. This technique modifies existing quantization techniques to ensure that sensitive operations like matrix multiplication and scalar addition produce valid, error-free results. To accommodate real-world precision constraints, we developed UQC specifically for integer-based quantization. Our experiments with UQC on a non-linear neural network revealed a precision range where the network maintained its original accuracy and a larger range where it could adapt with minimal training, showing its effectiveness in preventing subtle errors caused by hardware or data entry mistakes. To accommodate real-world precision constraints, we developed UQC specifically for integer-based quantization. Our findings highlight the potential of UQC to enhance the robustness of neural networks in application-specific settings. To achieve this efficiency, UQC requires significantly less training data and examples than other robust learning methods, demonstrating its value in numerous precision-based scenarios. Furthermore, our research discovered that UQC precedes other robust learning techniques in adapting to precise ranges, necessitating an automatic method to select ideal precision levels. To address this challenge, we developed another technique called Automatic Precision Selection (APS) that determines the most suitable precision level for each operation within a network by evaluating the trade-off between precision and network efficiency. Our experiments with APS on various networks revealed a precision range that minimizes the decrease in their accuracy when constrained, further showing its effectiveness in enhancing neural network robustness. We propose a novel, simple approach to enhance sequence tagging for under-resourced languages by leveraging structural information from the knowledge base. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method, we applied it to Russian name tagging, utilizing the Yandex Russian people database. Our proposal was implemented through a linear transition system and evaluated using the Seneca corpus, achieving a significant 5.5% gain in F-score over the baseline and outperforming the state-of-the-art approach for low-resource name tagging. Our method also compared favourably to deep learning baselines on the Seneca corpus, with results showing it performs competitively while being more efficient and simpler to implement. Our approach has the added benefit of producing readable and maintainable models, as evidenced by our experiment using randomly generated names, where our method accurately tagged 96.1% of the names despite having no prior training on that specific data. Our approach has a linear time complexity during inference, making it suitable for large-scale applications. Our method has the potential to be applied to other low-resource name tagging tasks in Slavic languages by adapting the training data to their specific naming conventions. Our research analyzed numerous sub-nuclear collisions' outcomes, specifically focusing on mid-rapidity p/π+ and K+/π+ ratios in LHC collisions at 7 and 13 TeV energies. Both ALICE and CMS experiments' data were utilized for this analysis. Initially, collisions' small size studies indicated no significant differences in p/π+ and K+/π+ ratios when compared to larger size collisions. However, as the number of participants increased in both LHC and RHIC collisions, ratios for p/π+ and K+/π+ exhibited similar trends regardless of collision size. Additionally, p/π+ and K+/π+ ratios demonstrated analogous behavior across various collision energies, all while displaying minimal change when compared to their corresponding reference ratios. Current research reveals minimal influence of collision size on strangeness content within final particle states, encouraged by phenomena's overall consistency across multiple experiments. Nonetheless, more precise measurements are needed to thoroughly understand this outcome, potentially illuminating any perceived lack of size dependence on particle ratios. Nonetheless, the lack of significant size dependence on particle ratios may also imply a lack of influence from initial state effects resulting from the high energy collisions. Our study suggested an essential need for further investigation into this perceived insensitivity to collision size, offering several possible approaches such as analyzing charged particle distributions with special attention to possible modifications resulting from initial state effects. In addition, our analysis revealed a sub-sensitivity of p/π+ ratio to collision size in heavy-ion collisions with large sizes, whereas a moderate sensitivity was observed in light-ion collisions with smaller sizes, potentially requiring further exploration into initial state effects resulting from high energy collisions. Our research utilized numerous event generators including MUSIC, AMPT, and MBT, to compare the outcomes with the analyzed data, showing that recently enhanced versions of models like MUSIC and AMPT failed to reproduce the observed outcome, whereas the older versions of the same models exhibited greater success. Ultimately, our study concluded that the strangeness content within final particle states at mid-rapidity p/π+ and K+/π+ ratios exhibit minimal change when varying collision size in high energy collisions, encouraged by phenomena's overall consistency across multiple experiments, while also offering several possible approaches to further investigate this perceived insensitivity to collision size. Our research also gathered sufficient data to create comprehensive figures of p/π+ and K+/π+ ratios across multiple collision energies with corresponding reference ratios, alongside charged particle yields with special attention to possible modifications resulting from initial state effects in heavy-ion and light-ion collisions with small and large sizes

We develop a symbolic decision procedure for determining if one regular expression is contained within another, based on Brzozowski's operator and the concept of regular expression rewriting with symbolic variables. This approach enables the automated assessment of safety properties defined using regular expressions in dynamically evolving systems, ensuring the inclusion of uncertain or dynamically changing patterns of behavior within specified boundaries. Specifically, we demonstrate the feasibility of symbolically determining inclusion within regular expressions by illustrating the method's applicability to evaluating inclusion within context-free languages defined by grammars with symbolic variables. We also examine the limitations of this approach and alternative methods for handling certain regular expression containment questions. Finally, we outline possible applications and extensions of this methodology, including the use of symbolic variables to enhance regular expression containment analysis for system call sequences. We further discover that this methodology can be refined to address the inclusion within context-free languages defined by grammars, a problem otherwise undecidable for context-free grammars and thus providing a significant contribution to the field. We demonstrate the efficacy of this methodology by applying it to a genuine system-related problem, namely the assessment of the inclusion within system call languages defined by recursive finite state machines, a problem otherwise considered intractable due to its high computational intensity. We significantly enhance the originally known result by showing that the inclusion within system call languages defined by recursive finite state machines is actually decidable through this methodology, a level of efficiency we measured by means of recursive finite state machine blowouts, a newly introduced parameter with units of bits per transition, and found it to be substantially lower than expected. We further observe that the application of this methodology to system call languages yields a level of efficiency directly proportional to the blowouts of the corresponding recursive finite state machines. We also examine the relationship between this efficiency and additional relevant metrics of these machines, exploring the possibility of using these machines with a higher level of complexity, such as extended recursive finite state machines, to determine the inclusion within system call languages defined by them, a problem otherwise considered to have an exponential time and space complexity, thus demonstrating the robustness of this methodology. We conclude by highlighting the versatility of this methodology, having the potential to enhance decision procedures for temporal logic properties, providing a promising foundation for the automated verification of systems with regularly defined behavior. We also outline possible avenues for further developing this methodology, including the use of weighted automata and the evaluation of weighted properties, the inclusion within taint propagation languages, and the verification of systems with regularly defined behavior in web services. Recently, VIO (Visual-Inertial Odometry) techniques have achieved high accuracy, albeit primarily using hand-crafted features. We propose a deep learning-based VIO framework, termed DeepVIO, that employs convolutional neural networks (CNN) to process both camera and inertial data. A specific design of DeepVIO, which we call the 'Shared-Graph Network', incorporates a graph neural network (GNN) to model state and covariance, varying from standard VIO by utilizing inertial signals in image processing. Experimental data shows that DeepVIO outperforms state-of-the-art methods on both indoor and outdoor datasets with both real-world and simulated inertial sensors. Moreover, DeepVIO's covariance estimation capability facilitates reliable state uncertainty calculation, setting it apart from other learning-based VIO techniques. We further investigate the efficacy of GNN's covariance estimation and state prediction in isolation to gain insight into the design of DeepVIO. Due to the complexity of estimating the graph's initial state and covariance, we propose an innovative method to train the GNN, which we term the 'learning-from-sparse-graph' training method, where the GNN is trained using sparse ground truth covariance matrices. Ultimately, this learning-based VIO framework and our proposed designs can serve as a foundation for enhancing the odometry estimation performance of various learning-based VIO models. We have publicly available code and datasets for reproducibility. We believe that this research contributes significantly to the development of learning-based VIO algorithms, especially those utilizing inertial sensors, which are inherently difficult to model and require more precise state and covariance estimation. This study investigates how different edge finite elements can be utilized to solve inverse problems where data is incomplete, specifically in the context of imaging and sensor networks. By utilizing the Cayley-Menger configuration theorem, we derive explicit edge length formulas for various elements, including $P_1$ and Paganini elements. We then apply these elements to solve an inverse problem in a sensor network, and finally, we utilize these elements to solve a tomography problem, both computationally and experimentally. We determine that the Paganini element provides the most precise results for both inverse problems, even when the distance deviations are as large as 50%. We also compare these results with those obtained using a least squares optimization method, and finally, we experimentally verify a data completion problem using a Paganini element-reconstructed grid, both with and without noise. We find that this element can accurately reconstruct a grid from incomplete data, even at high levels of noise, as demonstrated by the experimental results. We also obtain an exact reconstruction when the data is complete, whether it is simulated or experimental. We determine that this element can reduce the number of sensors required for a certain level of accuracy by up to 5.5 times, as confirmed by both computational and experimental data. We believe that this element has significant potential in real-world applications, such as imaging and sensor networks, due to its high precision, flexibility, and efficiency. The process of incorporating vast amounts of existing knowledge into a student model using relation extraction facts can be challenging.  We believe a better approach exists for teaching a student model to pay attention to specific input elements that relate to given facts.  In this approach, attention is directed to salient parts of the input in accordance with the factual target attributes, which we believe enhances the learning process for a student model.  To achieve this, we propose a novel attention mechanism called a Focused Transformer, where the student model is enabled to focus on specific elements of the input by adjusting the attention distribution.  We applied this method to a student model trained using relation extraction data and observed a significant improvement of 3.5% in accuracy over the existing state.  Additionally, Focused Transformer outperformed the current state in other attention mechanisms in relation extraction, with gains of 1.5% and 2.5% in relation extraction tasks using Wikipedia and WebText, respectively.  The code is publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/SeongUnYang/FocusedTransformer.  In the process of refining Focused Transformer, we discovered a sub-optimal issue where increasing the number of target attributes often results in a decrease in accuracy.  To address this, we developed a simple Proportional Sampling technique that prioritizes the uniform distribution of attention across target attributes by proportionally adjusting the attention weights.  This technique further enhanced the Focused Transformer with an additional accuracy gain of 0.5% in WebText.  The code for Proportional Sampling is also publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/SeongUnYang/FocusedTransformer.  We believe that focused attention can be beneficial for other text classification tasks involving additional features or labels, and encourage researchers to explore this idea further.  We also propose a simple yet effective approach to reduce the number of required target attributes for training, which we call the Partial Focus strategy, and demonstrate its applicability to real-world scenarios.  This strategy is adaptable to various industries and can be easily incorporated into existing pipelines with minimal additional costs.  The proposed methods are unique in that they leverage focused attention to tackle the challenges of training on massive datasets with numerous additional features or labels, and we anticipate their widespread adoption in industrial settings.  We have made the codes for Focused Transformer and Proportional Sampling publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/SeongUnYang/FocusedTransformer.  We have also made the data processing codes for WebText and Wikipedia publicly accessible on GitHub

In the unitary case, we find that the minimum distinguishability time exceeds half the system's decoherence time, and it's determined by the time it takes the system to lose memory of its initial state. In non-unitary dynamics, the concept of time becomes relative, but we define the minimum distinguishability time as the point at which the system's state ceases to differ significantly from its environment's state, which we mark as the beginning of the dephasing process. We develop a model where the interaction between the system and environment causes loss of correlation, and we show that the time it takes for the system to become indistinguishable from its environment is directly proportional to the system's decoherence rate, as well as the size of the environment, and we provide numerical examples to illustrate this behavior. Lastly, we investigate the time it takes for a system to become indistinguishable from its environment in a scenario with multiple environments, and we find that the minimum distinguishability time is the maximum of the times with each environment, which makes physical sense due to the condition that the system interacts with each environment for at least that long. Moreover, we find that the time it takes for the system to become indistinguishable from its environment is the slower of either the time it takes for the system to lose memory of its initial state or the time it takes for the system to reach its equilibrium state, which we mark as the point of steady state. We term the time it takes for the system to become indistinguishable from its environment the dephasing time, and we propose it as a useful concept in non-unitary dynamics. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for the coherence time of superposition states and the distinction time of non-unitary dynamics. The peculiar Type Ia supernova, SN~2020jfo, is reported to have exhibited exceptionally strong [Ni~II] and weak [Fe~II] line emissions in its spectrum, resulting in a notable nickel to iron abundance ratio above the solar value. This ratio is exceptionally high, with a ratio of 3.5~dex observed in SN~2020jfo, in contrast to the typical ratio of -1 to 1~dex seen in other Type Ia supernovae. The unique nickel and iron abundances in SN~2020jfo are further confirmed by the suppression of [Co~II] and [Ni~II] line strengths at 7.5 to 10 microns in its spectrum, as well as the rapid decline of its [Fe~II] line strength in the weeks following its explosion. The abundance of elements like cobalt, silver, and gold in SN~2020jfo are also estimated for the first time in a Type Ia supernova, with a calculated abundance of 0.3 to 1~dex for cobalt and less than -0.3~dex for silver and gold. The distinct chemical signature in SN~2020jfo is hypothesized to be the result of a super-asymmetrical explosion with a high energy release that caused the rapid mixing of nickel with iron, resulting in a nickel to iron ratio similar to that observed in certain hyper-nova remnants. The exceptional brightness of SN~2020jfo in the near-infrared spectrum, along with the abundance of elements like cobalt, silver, and gold, make it an intriguing object worthy of further theoretical and observational analysis. The peculiar chemical composition in SN~2020jfo is yet to be compared with the abundance of elements in other hyper-nova remnants, however its unique characteristics do make it a potential candidate for having a direct impact on the formation of massive star remnants. The distinct evolution of SN~2020jfo in the weeks following its explosion, along with the abundance of elements like cobalt, silver, and gold, make it an unusually comprehensive object of study for the community of supernova researchers. The research on SN~2020jfo highlights the unique opportunities for further analysis on the formation of massive star remnants presented by the explosion's scalar mixing of elements like nickel, iron, cobalt, silver, and gold, as well as the probable link between this explosion and hyper-nova remnants. We present a novel method to determine the azimuthal rotation angle of a cross-like image produced by a lobster-eye optics system, which features a rotatable azimuthal symmetry and is utilized in particle identification. The proposed approach analyzes the spatial distribution of the image and employs a pattern recognition method based on the fit coefficient of a specific function. The rotation angle is determined as the value that yields the highest fit coefficient. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach utilizing simulated data and a (dE--dE) versus (MIP--dE) representation, and further illustrate the method's applicability to varying signal thresholds. The results show that this approach accurately determines the rotation angle for different segments of the system, even in cases where the outer photodetector signals are close to the threshold, and it is robust against varying signal thresholds. The approach is found to be suitable for automatic rotation angle identification in real-time applications. The performance of this approach is assessed utilizing both the standard deviation and the mean of the rotation angle distribution. The proposed method exhibits a standard deviation of 0.21 radians in the most critical region of operation, which corresponds to a 2.4 mm gap between the inner and outer photodetectors in a specific setup. The corresponding mean rotation angle difference is 0.053 radians, which is equivalent to a 3.1 degree deviation over the 4 cm length of the system. The performance of this approach can be improved by adjusting the signal threshold, where a lower threshold results in a lower standard deviation of the rotation angle. The proposed method is a feasible solution for real-time applications requiring precise azimuthal rotation angle information, which is critical in systems with rotating components that affect the spatial distribution of the particle hits. The effectiveness of this approach has been validated utilizing both light and heavy ion beam experiments. The code utilized for this analysis is available upon request. The approach presented in this research can be utilized for other applications featuring rotating components with azimuthal symmetry. The optimized code for this research is available at https://github.com/alexei-k/rotation-angle-analysis. Our analysis of the 1D case involves using the method of characteristics to reveal its connection to the corresponding first-order equation. We then investigate the application of level set methods, obtaining a system of partial differential equations with the max or sup function as an unknown. We resolve this issue by using the Borel transform, which allows us to interpret this system as a combination of the original equation and its interaction with its shock waves. We use this interpretation to understand the occurrence of solutions to the Cauchy problem and those defined on a compact domain with discontinuous initial conditions. Accurately predicting the mass of dark matter halos is crucial for understanding the evolution of the universe. Despite advancements in object formation theory, predicting halo masses directly from the properties of density fields remains unfulfilled. To address this challenge, a density-based model using a neural density estimator was developed to forecast halo masses in a given density field. By training the model using cosmological simulations with specific amplitude of initial scalar perturbations, it was observed that using a density-only model leads to a halo mass prediction more accurate than one based on velocity and density, and significantly better than one based solely on density without corrections. For an N-body simulation with a particular resolution, features of the model, including neural network architecture and training data volume, were found to be crucial for its performance. Therefore, a reliable density-based approach for predicting halo masses efficiently is within reach using current simulation capabilities. Furthermore, this method has the potential to enhance halo finding algorithms that rely on a minimum mass threshold by identifying candidate halos with the correct mass in a density field. In addition, it was discovered that the approach can effectively recover missing halos, especially those with masses below the resolution limit of the simulation, providing a useful solution for unresolved halos. Finally, the accuracy of the model degrades gradually with increasing amplitude of initial scalar perturbations, suggesting its scalability to simulations with more complex structure formation patterns. In its current form, the model exhibits appealing capabilities for efficiently predicting the masses of dark matter halos throughout the evolution of the universe. To further improve the model, strategies for enhancing the simulation simulations, such as the effects of resolution on mass resolution, and the proposed approach are discussed. The model has been made available for use in the field. The Python code can be accessed via https://github.com/alexander-luo/neural-halo-formation. This involves assigning mass and specific angular momentum to elements in a way that differs from conventional techniques. In the classic approach, these properties are calculated as means of the fluid elements, but we now use the moments of the angular velocity distribution to calculate mass and the moments of the angular velocity and angular momentum distribution to calculate specific angular momentum. These new definitions enable the calculation of surface mass distribution, the migration rate of stars, and the mass loss history of rotating main sequence stars with improved accuracy. A key challenge in using structural learning methods for NLP tasks is the large amount of labeled data required, making it difficult to scale for new tasks and languages. This research explores the potential NLP applications of selective labeling, a technique that reduces data requirements by labeling only the most informative sentences. To optimize sentence ranking, we developed a method combining a cheap forward pass using a state-of-the-art transformer-based model alongside a score generator network. Our results indicate that this approach can effectively prioritize labeled sentences for minimal loss of performance. Specifically, we found that selectively labeling 20% of sentences leads to an acceptable 1.5-fold increase in labeling cost, which further decreases as more sentences are labeled. Our proposed approach demonstrates a minimum 1.5-fold reduction in data required to achieve the same performance as non-selective labeling, which we attribute to the effective distribution of labeled sentences. Our code has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/kuangshu/selective_labeling. Furthermore, our research highlights the potential benefits of selective labeling in tasks like text classification, where labeling all sentences is impractical due to their vast number, which we aim to investigate in greater depth as a future study. Our experiments used the Stanford Question Answering Dataset (SQuAD) to validate our approach, which we plan to expand on in the context of other datasets, including Multi-Step Question Answering Dataset (MSQA) and XQuAD. Our findings also suggest that selective labeling can simplify training by reducing labeling cost, which we believe holds true for a wide range of generating tasks. The simultaneous observation of gravitational and electromagnetic radiation during neutron star mergers has the potential to greatly enhance our understanding of these events. Although the first detection of gravitational waves from merging neutron stars was made in 2017, there have been no simultaneous observations of electromagnetic radiation from the same event. We examine the capabilities of current and future interferometric gravitational wave detectors for simultaneous observations of gravitational and electromagnetic radiation from neutron star mergers, considering the current limits of electromagnetic detection methods, including gamma-ray, X-ray, and optical observations. We calculate the maximum distances at which neutron star mergers could be simultaneously detected via gravitational waves and electromagnetic radiation within the next decade, taking into account the sensitivity improvements of advanced gravitational wave detectors and anticipated limits of electromagnetic radiation. We find that future detections of neutron star mergers through gravitational waves and simultaneous observations of electromagnetic radiation will primarily occur within the Milky Way, with the potential for several such detections per year in the next decade. We discuss the capabilities of future telescopes, such as the Square Kilometre Array, the next generation of X-ray and optical detectors, and the capabilities of gamma-ray satellites in the next decade, including the Advanced Imager on the Space Telescope, the X-ray Enhanced Survey and Mission, and the James Webb Space Telescope. We examine the capabilities of these future telescopes for detecting radiation from neutron star mergers at the detection limits of current instruments, considering the energy spectra of electron captives and interaction energies. We present the expected positions, distances, and luminosities of future detections of neutron star mergers, considering the capabilities of current and future telescopes, and the distribution of mergers within the Milky Way. We discuss the potential for the Square Kilometre Array to detect gravitational waves from neutron star mergers with the help of X-ray and optical observations, and the potential for the James Webb Space Telescope to detect radiation from mergers at the edge of the Milky Way. This ethnographic research explores the consequences of the 2020 pandemic on encounters between diverse community members in an urban setting.  Despite restrictions being lifted, a prolonged period of social distancing had significant impacts on the diversity of encounters in public spaces.  Residents found innovative ways to cultivate community resilience through supportive relationships in their neighborhoods.  One woman's initiative to distribute free food led to a strong sense of community among recipients and volunteers, demonstrating how marginalized people came together to support one another during this time.  Through attending church services, a pastor fostered a spirit of community by highlighting the importance of diversity, a value that had been compromised within the congregation.  A study of encounters in a urban setting reveals the complex dynamics of diversity within public spaces, highlighting how altered social interactions can either hinder or promote community resilience.  The 2020 pandemic exacerbated existing social divides, yet it also gave rise to innovative ways that urban dwellers came together to support one another.  The diversity of encounters in public spaces is shaped by the interplay between individual desires for social connections, community norms, and structural inequalities, influencing the levels of diversity found in urban settings. Around a young, massive star with a circumstellar disk, gravitational influence can cause objects to migrate toward the center, competing for dominance in a potentially unstable inner region. Computer simulations of a massive YMC with a massive companion suggest that migrating objects in a circumstellar disk could lead to instability in the inner disk, resulting in the formation of gaps and streams, and potentially even slowing the migration and allowing the inner disk to cool quickly. For a massive YMC without a massive companion, migrating objects in the form of small bodies and planetesimals can create multiple gaps in the disk, limiting the growth of massive planets and affecting the availability of material for eclispse disks. Similarly, in a massive YMC with a massive companion, the strong gravitational influence can produce numerous gaps, preventing massive planets from forming and influencing the characteristics of eclipse disks. Additionally, the massive YMC without a massive companion provides an possible explanation for the recently observed [NeII] emission in some YMCs, which was initially difficult to explain due to the abundance of neon in the outer galaxy. Similarly, the massive YMC with a massive companion offers an possible explanation for the recently observed chemical abundance patterns in some YMCs, which were initially difficult to explain due to the rapid mixing of elements in the inner regions. Computer simulations also suggest that in the massive YMC without a massive companion, the migration of small bodies and planetesimals can create conditions favorable for the formation of massive bar-like structures in the inner disk, which in turn could lead to the formation of massive binary stars. Similarly, in the massive YMC with a massive companion, the migration of small bodies and planetesimals can create conditions favorable for the formation of massive bar-like structures in the inner disk, which in turn could lead to the formation of massive binary stars and also produce oscillatory effects on the massive companion, potentially exacerbating its instability and leading to the ejection of the massive companion as a run-away star. Computer simulations also suggest that in the massive YMC without a massive companion, the migration of small bodies and planetesimals can create conditions favorable for the formation of massive binary stars and also produce oscillatory effects on the massive star itself, potentially exacerbating its instability and leading to the ejection of the massive star as a run-away star. Computer simulations also suggest that in the massive YMC without a massive companion, the migration of small bodies and planetesimals can delay the formation of massive planets in the inner regions of the disk and also limit the availability of material for eclipse disks.

This paper introduces a novel navigation system for mobile systems equipped with sonar sensors, designed to navigate in an underwater environment with a layered control framework. The system leverages a layered structure to guide its mobile platform to pre-defined goals, with a top-level controller navigating across broad areas and a more precise controller managing local sonar readings. By simplifying the controller network, this approach enhances navigation by eliminating the need for a comprehensive map of the surroundings. As a result, this method enables the mobile system to efficiently navigate through an underwater world with temporary obstacles, relying solely on real-time sonar data. Moreover, this approach fosters a more efficient and adaptable controller architecture, capable of handling time-constrained and dynamic sonar readings. To validate this method, we present simulation results showing its effectiveness in an increasingly complex underwater environment. Furthermore, we provide a basic implementation of this sonar navigation system using the ROS2 framework, along with advice for optimizing this method in real-world applications. Overall, this novel layered control framework presents a groundbreaking solution for sonar-based navigation in an underwater world, poised to inspire innovative applications across this domain. To facilitate further development and testing of this method, we offer the related code and simulation assets at this link https://github.com/AndresGomezBenitez/layered_sonar_navigation. In addition, we outline possible future enhancements to this method, including the incorporation of additional sensors, a more sophisticated controller architecture, and localization within more expansive underwater environments. With these enhancements, this novel navigation system can be refined to successfully navigate mobile systems through increasingly complex underwater scenarios. In the course of this research, we discovered that the term "topological navigation" was often used interchangeably with "topological control", although these terms have distinct meanings in the field of graph theory. Consequently, we propose that researchers adhere to a more precise classification of navigation systems based on their underlying mathematical foundations, drawing from the principles of topological theory. By embracing this shift in terminology, the navigation community can benefit from established theoretical frameworks and graphical models, thereby enhancing the development of reliable and efficient navigation systems. Finally, we emphasize the potential applications and advantages of using topological methods in navigation systems, highlighting the uniqueness of this approach in avoiding the pitfalls of metric-based navigation, where distance calculations can lead to errors and instability in control systems. By leveraging topological navigation, we can create more adaptable and resilient navigation systems capable of efficiently managing complex and dynamic underwater environments. We investigate the interplay of curvature effects, hysteresis, and phase transitions in dynamic systems with adaptive topologies, specifically in the context of a temporal network where the focus is on local perspective and curvature constraints. We introduce a model that leverages the concept of recency, adapting it to account for the curvature of the network, and integrate it into a dynamic system to explore its phase transitions and hysteresis. The model's simplicity allows us to analyze its underlying mechanics through the application of curvature-corrected techniques, including the curvature-corrected Legendre transform to analyze entropy changes and the hysteresis that emerges during dynamic processes. By examining the relationships between these processes, we gain insight into how the conditions that favor phase transitions and hysteresis also promote the breakdown of the recency effect. Consequently, this leads to a broader understanding of how the entropic hysteresis that arises from the interplay of curvature, adaptivity, and time can result in the dynamic system's inability to learn from past experiences. Ultimately, this research paves the way for a theoretical framework that can be extended to address more complex networks and adaptive systems with dynamic topologies. The model's limitations provide a useful foundation for future work aimed at exploring the interplay between curvature, time, and adaptivity in complex networks and dynamic systems. The findings presented here have implications for the analysis of phase transitions and hysteresis in biological networks, such as protein interaction networks, that evolve over time. The simplicity of the proposed model also offers a valuable benchmark for the development of more advanced theoretical frameworks that can be applied to the study of adaptive systems with dynamic topologies. We address the challenge of scalable solution methods for relaxation-based techniques that address the L1-PCA problem under circular symmetry. This implementation invites alternative optimization strategies for resolving the non-convex variation of the problem. Specifically, we examine a second-order cone program representing a rotationally invariant L1-PCA problem and present two methods for solving it: an ascending algorithm that generates successive approximations and is inspired by the method of alternating projections, and a gradient-based optimization approach utilizing the limited memory BFGS algorithm. We evaluate and compare the performance of both methods in resolving this representation in a range of scenarios featuring real and synthetic data sets. In these experiments, the ascending and BFGS algorithms are both shown to be effective in addressing the rotationally invariant L1-PCA problem, even in its original, non-relaxed form. We find that the ascending algorithm is more robust in handling larger, more complex datasets, whereas the BFGS algorithm is more efficient in resolving smaller-scale problems. We also observe that the BFGS algorithm is more prone to failure in addressing the original, non-relaxed problem, whereas the ascending algorithm is more successful in achieving the optimal solution in all problem instances. We propose a threshold-based stopping criterion for the ascending algorithm and examine its impact on the solution quality and the number of iterations required. We find that this criterion significantly enhances the solution quality at a minimal computational cost, whereas the increase in the number of iterations is relatively smaller. We further investigate the relationship between the rotationally invariant L1-PCA and the traditional L1-PCA without any restriction on the support size. Specifically, we examine how the performance of the proposed methods is affected by different upper and lower bounds on the support size. We find that both algorithms are more efficient in resolving problems with smaller support sizes, as predicted by the theoretical analysis presented in the introduction section. We find that the eigendecomposition-based approach yields the most stable and efficient representation, whereas the FFT-based approach yields the least stable and efficient representation. We propose a consistency-checking framework for validating large-scale annotations by framing the task as a search for consistent annotations through the lens of multiple translators. Given a particular semantic labeling task, such as identifying product names in web text, we find that a paraphrase-based method can produce reliable results when the task involves categorizing semantic categories like entities or parts of speech, but this approach is less effective for tasks like name extraction. In such cases, a combination of automatic evaluation metrics like F-score or embedding-based distances is necessary to enhance consistency checking. We further explore integrating additional annotation characteristics into the framework, including annotated relation extraction and sentiment classification. Our approach demonstrates improved performance even for more intricate tasks like sentiment classification, achieving a significant gain of 5% F-score with only 100 paraphrase pairs, and this improvement persists with larger annotation sets. Our framework facilitates a linear scaling effect, with a particular advantage for large datasets (>10,000 annotations). We additionally analyze the relationship between annotation cost, consistency checking difficulty, and the scalability of our approach, and provide theoretical and empirical insights into this interconnection. Our consistency-checking framework is designed to be adaptable for various semantic labeling tasks and annotated data, and we anticipate its utility in a broad spectrum of applications. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghru/consistency_checking. ViAMNav introduces a novel method called HiTMap to guide robots through complex environments with limited knowledge of the layout by leveraging the power of Hamiltonian Path Finding. Unlike conventional metric maps, HiTMap prioritizes efficient navigation by simplifying the underlying graph of the environment, turning what would be a challenging problem into a more manageable path-finding challenge. By representing the layout as a set of localized components, HiTMap significantly reduces navigation costs while requiring only a limited amount of sensory input. Through simulated simulations, HiTMap demonstrates improved performance compared to other state-of-the-art methods, especially in open spaces with minimal obstacles, and has the added benefit of being a real-time controller with no need for map relocalization. Moreover, HiTMap is shown to excel in navigating through scenarios with moving obstacles and sparely populated environments. Additionally, it is observed that HiTMap successfully avoids local minima and delivers high-quality solution trajectories in a short amount of time. The validity of its algorithmic framework is validated through comparative studies against existing global metric mapping solutions using various motion planning scenarios and parameters. The project's source code is available for public use on GitHub at https://github.com/robotology/ViAMNav. The related research paper can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.02867.
