We achieved a record sensitivity in detecting a local magnetic field using atomic interferometry, at a level of $10^{-13}$Tesla, which surpasses the quantum limit. This accomplishment was made possible by utilizing spin-polarized, hyperfine structure-free $^{1}^{7}O$ atoms, interacting for one second at $10^{4}$ times their de Broglie wavelength, and was demonstrated in an arrangement where the magnetic field's effect on the interferometer's phase resulted in a signal that exceeded the noise of both the magnetic sensitivity and the quantum limit by at least ten times. Furthermore, our measurement revealed that local magnetic fields as weak as $10^{-12}$Tesla could be stably maintained for extended periods. Ultimately, our research highlighted the capability of atomic interferometry to reach magnetic sensitivities beyond the quantum limit, and demonstrated that even weaker magnetic sensitities, beyond those already achieved, are feasible using this method. Additionally, our findings emphasized the significance of precisely controlling magnetic fields when using atomic interferometry, and demonstrated that even minimal residual magnetic fields in the experiment's environment could be detected, including fields as weak as $10^{-14}$Tesla in the laboratory setting. Lastly, our magnetic sensitivity, exceeding $10^{-13}$Tesla for one second at $10^{4}$ times the de Broglie wavelength, is the most sensitive detection achieved to date, surpassing even gravitational measurements using atomic interferometry. The minimum detectable value of a local gravitational field gradient, which we also set, at $2\times 10^{-8}$m$^{-1}$s$^{-2}$ for one second at $10^{4}$ times the de Broglie wavelength, constitutes the most sensitive detection of this parameter to date. The development of this record-breaking measurement was facilitated by breakthroughs in source technology, beam manipulation, and atomic polarization, as well as innovative use of spin-symmetric and spin-antisymmetric interference patterns in the $^{1}^{7}O$ ground state doublet. The techniques refined during this research have implications for atomic interferometry using other rare isotopes, and could be applied to using $^{1}^{7}O$ in atomic physics applications such as atomic clocks and quantum computation. The effectiveness of using atomic interferometry for detecting very weak local magnetic fields has been demonstrated, and this method is now capable of breaking the quantum limit for sensitive magnetic field detection, as well as offering prospects for rare isotopes. The record-breaking sensitivity achieved in this research has significant implications for atomic physics

We investigate a Bayesian model that employs a Dirichlet process for density priors in a mixed modeling framework. Within this framework, we demonstrate that the model's current formulation results in a lack of uniqueness in the estimation of admixture weights. To address this issue, we develop a method that leverages the Dirichlet process's parametrization in terms of stick-breaking representations. By manipulating the representation and utilizing the posterior samples from a Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm, we can derive an efficient procedure for recovering the identifiable admixture weights. Furthermore, this approach enables us to conduct posterior inference on the admixture weights and the density function. We validate our proposed method through numerical experiments and a real-world application. Additionally, we provide a theoretical analysis of the proposed method's performance. To facilitate practical implementation, we have made the code available publicly. We also outline possible future directions for extending this research, including exploring its applications in imaging and genetic analysis. Traditional GPU memory allocators undergo significant performance declines when managing small-scale memory allocations commonly encountered in dynamic graph-based networks, even with abundant global memory available, due to limited on-chip memory.  To address this challenge, we present DynaSOAr, a highly efficient, fully on-chip memory allocator tailored for SPMD architectures, leveraging local memory for fast, low-latency allocation operations.  Our key innovation involves splitting on-chip memory into multiple distinct pools, each with a unique size and purpose, and employing a multi-level allocation hierarchy to maximize pool utilization and reduce memory waste.  We demonstrate DynaSOAr's exceptional performance and memory management, showcasing a 3.1x speedup and 5x reduction in memory waste when implementing a real-world graph neural network application, and a 2x speedup and 20x reduction in memory waste when running a randomised stress test on a real-world dataset.  Our findings highlight the substantial benefits of using a dedicated memory allocator that is entirely self-contained on-chip, without the need for frequent global memory accesses, and demonstrate DynaSOAr's versatility across various real-world graph neural network applications.  Our code is available at https://github.com/JasonZeng/DynaSOAr.  Our approach can be applied to various SPMD architectures, including NVIDIA's A100 and Amazon Web Services' AWS F1.  Our discovery underlines the substantial advantages of using a dedicated, fully on-chip memory allocator, without the need for frequent global memory accesses, and highlights the significance of optimising memory allocators for deep learning applications with limited on-chip memory. The impact of spin-orbit coupling on local states associated with magnetic adatoms or dimer defects within a otherwise non-magnetic 2D lattice is theoretically examined using a tight-binding model. We analyze the defect state's energy levels in both clean and disordered lattices, considering both monolayer and bilayer graphene and hBN. The results indicate that the spin-orbit coupling causes the YSR state's energy levels to shift and shift the energy where the YSR states' peak appear. When there are multiple YSR states, the spin-orbit coupling can also cause the energy levels to become entangled, leading to the disappearance of some YSR state peaks. Furthermore, the presence of the substrate can cause the energy levels to shift, but the spin-orbit coupling's effect on the YSR states remains unchanged. Additionally, the presence of the zero-energy YSR state depends on the number of electrons on the adatom or dimer and its momentum. Finally, the proposed model is compared to experimental HEED spectra, showing good agreement when the spin-orbit coupling is taken into account. The proposed model also predicts that the YSR state's energy levels will shift when there are two YSR states present. The proposed model is a general framework that can be applied to a wide range of 2D lattices with strong spin-orbit coupling. The spin-orbit coupling's effect on the YSR states' energy levels is so significant that it can alter the outcome of experiments designed to detect zero-energy YSR states. The presence of zero-energy YSR states has been reported in multiple experiments, but the spin-orbit coupling's effect on these states was not considered, leading to some of the outcomes being misinterpreted. The proposed model provides a clear understanding of how the spin-orbit coupling affects the YSR states' energy levels, offering a potential explanation for some of the outcomes reported in experiments where the spin-orbit coupling was not considered. The model's limitations are also examined by comparing the results obtained using the proposed model with those obtained using the Anderson model, showing that the two models predict different energy level spectra. However, both models predict that the energy levels will shift when there are two YSR states present. The proposed model is a simple model that assumes that the spin-orbit coupling and on-site energy are the only significant interactions between the adatom or dimer and the lattice, but it is a robust model that can be applied to a wide range of 2D lattices with strong spin-orbit coupling

Qubits are the fundamental units of information in quantum computers, and their mass has been found to vary depending on the type of error, unlike qutrits which remain unaffected. In this research, we examined the impact of random gauge noise on qubits and qutrits in different scenarios, finding that their masses behave contrastingly under coherent and decohencent processes. While qubit mass becomes distorted even further under noise, its tolerance to noise is comparable to qutrits under specific conditions. Additionally, we developed a qutrit model utilizing the Dirac equation, which enabled us to precisely determine the mass of qutrits even in the presence of noise. We also discovered that the noise tolerance of qutrits can be enhanced by entangling multiple qutrits, differing from qubits that are actually perturbed by multi-qubit connections. Our innovative approach to mass calculation through the use of Wigner functions also facilitates the visualization of their entropy patterns as well as their reliance on error-channels. Our study paves the way for utilizing mass as a gauge-invariant metric in assessing the performance and noise-tolerance of various quantum systems. We investigate how polynomial diameter in finite groups is influenced by the distribution of their conjugacy classes and nilpotent subgroups. Initially, we demonstrate that for a group with a polynomial diameter of $d^n$ for $n > 1$, there exists a upper bound on the number of conjugacy classes that can be both small and abundant, i.e., both less than $d^n$ and significantly greater than $n$. Furthermore, in a group with a polynomial diameter of $d^n$ for $n \geq 1.5$, we find that there are constraints on the size of nilpotent subgroups that can be both large and abundant, i.e. both greater than $d^n$ and significantly less than $n$. Lastly, we establish that within a class of groups defined by a specific set of properties, those with polynomial diameter are precisely those with a bounded diameter. We also provide some discussions on finite groups characterized by a polynomial diameter of $d^n$ for $n \geq 1$, focusing on cases where this is achieved through a polynomial growth in conjugacy classes or a polynomial growth in nilpotent subgroups. Ultimately, our investigation leads to an in-depth examination of the symmetric group $S_n$, demonstrating how its diameter evolves with an increase in $n$ and how it scales compared to $n$. We discover that the diameter of $S_n$ follows a more complex pattern, but it is guaranteed to be at least $\Omega(n^{1-2/\log n})$ for $n \geq 6$, while missing a matching upper bound of $O(n^{3.5})$ for $n \geq 5$. We conclude by highlighting the vastness of the symmetric group's diagram due to its extremely dense middle levels, attributing this density to the presence of numerous nilpotent subgroups that significantly contribute to its diameter. We propose the establishment of a new research directory, Finite Diameter Group Theory (FDGT), which we envision will undergo considerable growth in the future. We also outline some possible research directions within FDGT, including analyzing the diameter of specific groups of considerable significance, such as classical groups, simple groups, and solvable groups, as well as exploring the relationships between group diameter and other mathematical domains like number theory, combinatorial design theory, and computational complexity theory. Moreover, we believe that the development of efficient algorithms for determining the diameter of finite groups will be crucial for advancing in this field. This sensor utilizes a low-noise, high-gain amplifier and succeeds in precision temperature measurement without relying on digital signal processing. Unlike conventional approaches, it eschews conversion into digital form, instead employing analog-to-analog conversion to determine temperature. This design's simplicity is further highlighted by its minimal component count. Unlike other thermal sensors, it requires zero calibration, yet achieves outstanding performance even in the presence of intense light interference. Typical operating conditions include a supply voltage of 1.5V and a supply current of 1.7mA. This sensor's performance is remarkably impressive, with an exceptional performance-to-complexity ratio. Its applicability is vast, making it suitable for diverse automotive and industrial applications. Furthermore, its minimal component count facilitates easy integration into a variety of platforms via standard foundry processes. This temperature sensor's exceptional characteristics are showcased through comprehensive simulations using 90nm and 180nm process models, in addition to experimental results utilizing a 180nm test chip. Lastly, potential implementations in embedded systems are illustrated with the temperature sensor integrated into a microcontroller and an application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC).

We introduce the notion of a topological groupoid extension with a specified covering property and show it is equivalent to a gerbe over a topological stack for certain conditions. This extends the similarity between category-like objects and gerbes observed in topological physics by Simons and Szabo by also accounting for the underlying topological stack. In the process, we redefine the structure maps of a topological groupoid extension to align with Atiyah's gerbe framework and in the course of this redefinition, we discover all topological groupoid extensions with the specified property can be expressed as gerbes of actions. Futhermore, a relationship between etale topological groupoid extensions and etale gerbes over topological stacks is identified. Additionally, we discover all topological stack extensions can be expressed as gerbe extensions. Lastly, we outline the potential applications of these findings in topological condensed matter and quantum field theory.

A statistical analysis of molecular cores in the Perseus and Ophiuchi regions reveals a paradox: even though many cores with significant masses (above 10 solar masses) exist, few of them give birth to massive stars.  A theoretical model suggesting the mass growth of cores is random and uninfluenced by massive star formation is challenged by this observation.  Instead, the available data indicate that the relationship between the mass of a core and the mass of the massive star it forms is scale-invariant, suggesting that the process of massive star formation is governed by self-similar rules, not purely by chance.  As evidence, even when the mass of a core is corrected for the surrounding environment, the resulting relationship still appears self-similar.  Furthermore, even when considering the mass function of massive star-formed cores without correction, the resulting curve fits the classic self-similar model accurately.  These findings support the dynamic model proposed by Shu, Adams, and Lizano, which accurately explains the scale-invariant relationship between cores and massive star-formed probability density functions.  Both the mass growth of cores and massive star-formed probabiity density functions follow self-similar patterns, even when considering various environments.  Consequently, the term "0.068 solar masses per year" can be considered a typical core mass growth rate anywhere in massive star-forming regions.  Similarly, a core mass of 9.2 solar masses is now regarded as the most common mass for producing massive stars, rather than the upper limit initially thought.  Additionally, the most frequent massive star-formed mass has shifted from 60 solar masses to 20-40 solar masses, with a more even distribution below 20 solar masses. Comparing the ratio of CCH to CN derivatives in cyclopentadiene and benzene reveals a higher abundance of CN derivatives in cyclopentadiene, consistent with theoretical predictions showing more extensive ring opening for cyclopentadienyl than phenyl radicals. This is further demonstrated by the higher abundance of CCH derivatives in benzene, which results from the smaller ring strain causing less extensive bond breaking during cycloaddition. These findings support theoretical models showing that ring strain facilitates cycloaddition reactivity in small ring compounds like cyclopentadiene and norbornadiene. Additionally, both CCH and CN derivative abundances correlate with predicted mode reactivity, which is most significant for the CCH derivative at 399nm and the CN derivative at 540nm. This is particularly true for benzene, which exhibits the smallest ring strain and the strongest correlation with mode reactivity, providing a suitable compound for studying vibrational mode reactivity in a isolated environment. In cyclopentadiene, the larger standard deviation of the CN derivative abundance ratio with mode reactivity indicates a greater degree of cycloaddition reactivity with ring strain. Lastly, both CCH and CN derivative abundances decrease with increasing distance from the ring, which is more pronounced for the CCH derivative at 285nm, which is more sensitive to changes in ring reactivity due to larger bond dissociation energies. This is consistent with theoretical predictions showing that the 285nm mode corresponds to bond breaking and the 540nm mode corresponds to bond formation. Consequently, this study confirms the utility of CCH and CN derivative abundances as indicators of vibrational mode reactivity in cyclopentadienyl and phenyl compounds. We propose a novel attention mechanism called look-ahead attention for enhancing neural machine translation systems. This mechanism enables the current decoding step to draw attention to specific elements of the target sentence that the future decodings will focus on, allowing the model to produce more informed hypotheses and steer clear of dead ends. We experiment with several variations of look-ahead attention and find that incorporating forward look-ahead attention, where the model is allowed to attend to ungenerated parts of the target sentence during generation, yields substantial gains in performance. We further investigate the potential of long-looking attention, where the model is permitted to attend to both generated and ungenerated parts of the target sentence, and observe significant improvements in certain cases. Our implementation details include intra-neural network optimizations and a targeted sentence ranking approach for reducing the search space, and we conduct extensive experiments on publicly available NMT datasets. Our results demonstrate the efficacy of look-ahead attention and provide valuable insights for future enhancements. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghru/lookahead-attention. Our best model achieves a 13.0 BLEU score on WMT14 English-to-German, an improvement of 1.4 BLEU scores over the baseline. Our code is also applicable to other machine translation tasks. A dark energy model is proposed to explain the cosmic expansion acceleration by incorporating a viscous cosmological model into the framework of f(R) gravity. The $f(R)\eta$ gravity theory is used to describe the evolution of the universe, where $R$ represents the Ricci curvature and $\eta$ symbolizes the viscosity coefficient. The proposed model is then applied to analyze the dynamics of universe expansion powered by dark energy, specifically in the context of the $\Lambda$CDM model. The solutions obtained for the viscosity coefficient $\eta$ and the $f(R)$ function $f$ are found to be solvable, and the model's viability is tested through the visitosity coefficient's evolution from the present day to the big bang, along with an examination of the model's stability by computing the viscosity coefficient's average value. The model's performance is evaluated through a fit of its variables to observational data spanning $1200 < z < 0$, and the findings indicate that the proposed model exhibits the same growth characteristics as $\Lambda$CDM, while the viscosity coefficient $\eta$ is discovered to be essentially constant across time, featuring a minor deviation from $0$ of $1.01 \pm 0.01$ at the present day. The model's effectiveness in explaining the universe's expansion is confirmed by the fit results, and the study suggests that the proposed model offers a promising explanation for the universe's evolution, even with the introduction of a constant viscosity coefficient. The proposed model is found to satisfy the conditions of the weak energy theorem and the model's stability is confirmed through an examination of the viscosity coefficient's marginal change over time. The proposed model provides specific predictions for the viscosity coefficient $\eta$ and the $f(R)$ function $f$, which can be validated through observations of the cosmic microwave background and the large scale structure of the universe. The study demonstrates that a constant viscosity coefficient $\eta$ is sufficient to explain the universe's evolution effectively, even as the model adheres to the constraints of the weak energy condition and exhibits stability across time. The model's limitations are discussed, along with suggestions for enhancing the model by introducing a variable viscosity coefficient $\eta$ that changes with the universe's density and temperature. The proposed model opens doors for investigating the impact of viscosity on the evolution of the universe in the context of $f(R)\eta$ gravity, and the findings encourage a re-examination of the cosmic evolution paradigm with a viscosity-based approach. Our research introduces MFSSA, a novel method for adapting the Signal Separation Method for the Blind Identification Problem to multiple signal components. Initially developed by Cichocki and Blondel, this method leverages the idea of separating individual signals from mixed measurements by exploiting the uniqueness of signals' time-frequency patterns. We demonstrate MFSSA's versatility by applying it to diverse real-world data, including a simple temperature curve model and a high-resolution remote sensing image, in addition to synthetic data. Our results show that MFSSA effectively recovers multiple embedded signals, even in short-duration measurements with high sampling rates, and is robust to various interference levels and signal frequency spacings. Furthermore, MFSSA demonstrates robust performance in noisy, real-world applications, making it a valuable tool for analyzing temperature curves and remote sensing images. Our work also contributes to the field of blind source separation in time and frequency domains by providing multiple signal component separation algorithms and comparing their performance in challenging scenarios. Our research code is available online for the community to use and modify. Our future work aims to extend MFSSA for solving the blind source separation problem in more complex scenarios and with more realistic time-frequency signal representations. Our findings also suggest that the minimum allowable frequency spacing between signals can be indicative of a region with reduced noise in remote sensing images, paving the way for their practical application. Our approach provides a valuable solution for extracting specific information from mixed measurements in various real-world contexts, giving it considerable practical value. Our work is premised on the assumption that distinct signals within a measurement have varying time-frequency patterns, making it suitable for use on signals in the time-frequency domain, including those obtained through the use of the continuous wavelet transform. Our research demonstrates that MFSSA is a reliable and efficient method for signal extraction in various settings by conducting extensive numerical experiments, along with the practical application of extracting information from a remote sensing image of a temperature curve. This study utilizes an optimization technique for plasma sources, specifically the M2 multi-disc plasma source, which is utilized in the JIPLC device. We used an genetic algorithm to optimize the source's parameters with the goal of maximizing electron temperature while ensuring a minimum electron density of 5 x 10^10 particles per cubic meter. The algorithm's effectiveness was evaluated by creating a grid of results covering possible source configurations. It was found that the algorithm efficiently identified the optimal configuration for maximum electron temperature, which corresponded to the highest density meeting the set criteria. The optimization process considered various Limmer electrode lengths, widths of the central electrode, plasma volume, and pressure. The resulting optimal configuration had an electron temperature of 4.55 kWh, density of 7.45 x 10^10 particles per cubic meter, and was achieved with specific source dimensions. The methodology provided can be applied to other plasma sources. The technique helps source parameters that maximize plasma properties, and the example given shows that even in cases where there are many local optimums, genetic algorithms can effectively find the global optimum. The need to carefully select the population size, number of generations, and mutation rate for the algorithm to produce consistent results with the current setup is also emphasized. The JIPLC device, which utilizes the M2 plasma source, requires a plasma density of at least 5 x 10^10 particles per cubic meter for correct operation, and the optimization process helps determine the required plasma properties for the device to function correctly. The method given can be applied to other plasma sources with different parameters, and it is also applicable to other devices that rely on plasma sources. The paper the knowledge of which is presented here also notes the relationship between the M2 plasma source's dimensions and its ability to produce plasma, and it shows that only a limited set of the source's possible configurations can produce the required electron density. We introduce Graph Convolution Aliases (GCA), a novel interpretation of Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs). This framework reconsiders the relationship between traditional Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and fully connected Neural Networks, revealing their equivalence to Graph Convolutional Networks in specific spectral domains. We demonstrate the applicability of GCA to Convolutional Neural Networks, Fully Connected Neural Networks, and Graph Convolutional Networks, providing a unified understanding of these networks as graph convolutions in respective spectral domains. We also leverage this framework to enhance the performance of GCNs, resulting in a novel Graph Convolution Aliases Neural Network. This model achieves superior performance compared to current state-of-the-art GCN models on several datasets, including PubMed and NCI-1. This paper introduces a novel specification checking framework for evaluating the accuracy and reliability of software, which utilizes formal logical expressions to define conditions for correctness and safety. We developed a distinctive category of pseudocode, termed "strong pseudocode," specifically designed to address potential pitfalls of traditional pseudocodes, such as incomplete or misleading information for the purpose of specification checking. We demonstrated the effectiveness of our framework by applying it to an intricate real-world example, the Linux kernel's memory management using slab memory management, which comprises approximately 150 files and 5000 pseudocode statements. Our results showed that we could successfully identify and correct several critical errors within this slab memory management module, including two that could lead to memory leaks and over a dozen that could cause deadlocks, demonstrating the utility of our framework in ensuring the correctness of software through formal methods. Our approach provides an adaptable solution for validating complex, high-profile software systems, even when they lack an official formal specification, using only their source code. We also compared our methodology with the methods used to test the Linux kernel, which rely on targeted tests and manual code reviews, finding that our approach allows for a more precise guarantee of safety and correctness, although it would require significant resources for large-scale applications like the Linux kernel. Nonetheless, we highlight the potential of this methodology for a wide range of software systems that, unlike the Linux kernel, are more amenable to manual code review and targeted testing, such as device drivers and web applications, for which we provide concrete examples and trial results. Our framework and associated tools are part of the SpecCram suite, an open-source collection of software validation tools that can be accessed through https://www.speccram.org/. Our research was supported by the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada (NSERC) and the Alberta Innovates Technology Futures (AITF). We used the Frama-C static analysis platform for our experiments, which were conducted on computers running Linux with an Intel Core i7 processor and 64 GB of RAM. Our biggest project, the Linux kernel's memory management using slab memory management, required approximately 12 days to validate. We believe that our methodology provides a promising solution for the scalability problem associated with formal methods for software validation, even for large and complex applications. Our approach and the associated tools come with no licensing restrictions, allowing them to be freely used, modified, and distributed according to the terms of the GNU General Public License (GPL). We also made a video presentation of our research, which is accessible through the following link: https://www.youtube.com

We develop a first-ever one-pass algorithm for creating a coreset for the $k$-means clustering problem. This coreset can solve problems of significantly higher sizes than previously possible, reducing the required computations by roughly an order of magnitude. Our approach leverages a novel approach called "center shifting" that allows us to efficiently identify and circumvent areas with excessively complex data sets. By achieving a significant decrease in size, we can apply existing multi-pass coreset strategies that typically require more extensive computations. Our algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated through thorough computational simulations conducted using real-world and artificially generated data sets. These results show our one-pass algorithm delivers the most convincing performance improvements when addressing large-scale $k$-means clustering problems. Our algorithm is available for use as an open-source tool as part of the SnapPy software for graph theory computations. Our coreset construction algorithm has far-reaching implications, extending beyond the $k$-means clustering problem to various other mean-shift models, including those defined by user-specified distance functions, point processes, and spatial dynamics models. In large-scale grid worlds, efficient decision-making is crucial for navigating and evading other agents. A common approach to simplifying this process is to divide the world into sub-states, but how this benefits decision-making in pursuit-evasion scenarios, especially with multiple pursuers and evaders, has not been well-documented. We present a novel method to dynamically partition the world into larger sub-states, which we call superstates, and a planning algorithm to generate navigational commands based on these superstates. Our results show that using superstates improves decision-making efficiency, especially in sprawling environments, and our approach performs better than existing state-splitting methods that rely on static grid partitioning. Furthermore, our superstate approach is adaptable, reusable, and efficient, making it suitable for dynamic, high-stakes decision-making in complex grid worlds. We demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our superstate approach through comprehensive simulations of pursuit-evasion games in various grid scenarios. Our code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/alexforbes/superstates.

A theoretical framework that generates universal corrections to W and Z boson parton distribution functions (PDFs) has been developed for use in deep inelastic scattering and Drell-Yan processes at high energies. Within the EFT approach, known relations between collinear and weak collinear modes are established through evolution equations, enabling the extraction of effective PDFs that incorporate beyond-leading logarithmic accuracy. A key discovery in this research revealed that beyond NNLO QCD corrections can be factored into an expansion of universal corrections to PDFs, in conjunction with an expansion of the strong coupling constant. Consequently, the impact of these universal corrections can be significant at next-to-next-to-next-to-leading order, thereby highlighting the importance of incorporating them into predictions involving W and Z bosons. A suitable option for incorporating these universal corrections into PDF fits has been demonstrated using a fit to data from LEP, SMC, TEVATRON, and ILC experiments, and the resulting fit has been applied to make predictions for LHC and ILC processes. A key aspect explored in this research was the dependence of universal corrections on the choice of renormalization and factorization scales, along with an examination of their impact on hadron decay widths in low-energy scenarios. Furthermore, the development of an efficient numerical integration tool was undertaken to facilitate the incorporation of higher-order corrections into PDF fits and the prediction of physical processes. The methods constructed in this research have been designed to accommodate eventual incorporation of higher-order corrections beyond NNLO QCD, in conjunction with NLO electroweak corrections. The relevant code has been incorporated into public PDF sets, where the underlying methodology has been outlined in detail, along with suggestions for future development. The findings presented in this research have been applied to make predictions for a range of high-energy processes and heavy flavor tag rates in the EFT approach, utilizing realistic PDF fits fitted to a combination of LEP, SMC, TEVATRON, and ILC data, and have been used to examine the impact of W and Z boson PDFs on these processes. The relevant projects, code, and datasets are publicly accessible as part of the TIOGA package. The discovery of universal corrections has motivated an initiative to update the existing fitting code used for PDF fits, in conjunction with an examination of the relevant scale dependence, and has facilitated the development of a more general method for incorporating non-standard PDFs into fits. The research has been conducted as part of the TIOGA project, a comprehensive project aimed at achieving beyond NNLO QCD

To address this problem, we propose a multi-dynamics model that consists of multiple separate models, each trained to estimate the dynamics of a single task. To maximize efficiency, we reduce the ensemble to a competitive set of models based on their in-ensemble performance, ensuring the subset provides improved overall effectiveness. To facilitate the efficient learning of distinct dynamics models and reduce memory usage, we implement memory-efficient LSTM networks. Experimental evaluations conducted on various datasets reveal our proposed framework to be highly versatile and scalable, capable of handling a wide range of scenarios with a high degree of success. Specifically, our proposed method achieves notable improvements in both expert-level navigation in the DeepMind Lab and the complex multi-task control of Vizdoom, two notoriously difficult reinforcement learning scenarios. Observations of the millisecond pulsar PSR B1133+16, spanning 24 years, reveal the absence of visible scattering material around the pulsar. Our sample includes 132 individual scattering encounters with the pulsar, accounting for up to 13% of its on-line observations. Notably, the scattering screens lie along the line of sight to the pulsar, extending from the pulsar's distance (1.77 kpc) to several kiloparsecs beyond, indicating a significant void around this pulsar. We estimate the all-space scattering density at this line of sight to be 0.13 kpc$^{-1}$, significantly lower than expected based on the Large Magellanic Cloud survey, and attribute this to a lack of stars within the pulsar's scattering volume. Furthermore, the limited scattering at this line of sight compared to others at similar distances suggests that the distribution of scattering material is not uniform throughout the Galactic bulge. We calculate the probability of not observing scattering around this particular pulsar for the duration of its observation and consider possible explanations, including the pulsar's location within a planetary system's scattering disk, a surrounding nebula, a massive star missing the effects of a supernova explosion, or a void within the Galactic bulge. Lastly, this research provides a basis for future monitoring of this pulsar, potentially revealing any changes in the scattering environment. The scattering data can also be used to refine the pulsar's distance and the scattering density along its line of sight. VGG-SS, a comprehensive audio source reconstruction benchmark tailored for end-to-end neural source separation models, has been developed. This dataset surpasses previous benchmarks in several ways: it encompasses a diverse range of sources (over 32 distinct categories) reconstructed from over 5000 long audio files; each containing approximately 10 seconds of noise from a single source in a real-world environment, without any post-processing. Initially, VGG-SS was designed to assess the ability of a state-of-the-art neural source separation model to accurately reconstruct audio sources with a vast spectral span. Notably, VGG-SS outperforms SS-Tiny by a significant margin in terms of mean source reconstruction similarity (MSRS), using both clean and noisy data. Moreover, VGG-SS demonstrates improved performance when compared to other existing datasets in source separation tasks, including the Freesound Database and the MagnaTagATune Dataset. Additionally, VGG-SS exhibits a distinct advantage when employed in a single-source automatic music tagging task, as it surpasses the performance of both MagnaTagATune Dataset and the Freesound Database in this regard. The benchmark's limitations are also addressed by introducing VGG-SS-4D, a multi-source audio reconstruction dataset consisting of approximately 2000 short audio files, each lasting 4 seconds and containing 4 distinct sources from different spectral spans. The development of VGG-SS-4D highlights the challenge of modeling source spectra spans and highlights potential future research in this area. The proposed VGG-SS benchmark is suitable for evaluating single-source separation models and demonstrates a significant advantage over existing datasets in this domain. The research underlying VGG-SS is a preliminary step in a larger project aimed at creating a multi-source and multi-span speech separation dataset and benchmark. The current version of VGG-SS is available for public use on GitHub at the specified URL. This paper introduces Lorentzian Graph Convolutional Network (LGCN), the first model that leverages complex hyperbolic graphs for both node classification and graph generation tasks. LGCN enhances existing hyperbolic GCNs in both theoretical representation learning and practical performance. Specifically, it demonstrates improved performance in comparison to conventional GCNs, surpassing state-of-the-art results on real-world datasets for both tasks. Additionally, LGCN achieves superior results in comparison to other hyperbolic GCNs on various datasets, showcasing its broad applicability. This article provides a stability theorem for the inverse problem of determining the sound speed's variation from scattering data in an inverse problem involving the 2D Helmholtz equation. Unlike the one-dimensional case, where stability is achieved through a direct method, we employ a nonlinear operator theoretic approach to achieve the desired result in two dimensions. Specifically, we employ a Carleman estimate to establish an observability inequality, which, in turn, enables us to establish the desired stability result and, as a byproduct, obtain an improved constant for an existing inequality. Ultimately, this yields the desired geometric uniqueness result (i.e., the ability to determine the sound speed's variation from local scattering data) for the 2D Helmholtz equation. Additionally, we obtain analogous results for the 3D Helmholtz equation and the 2D Schroedinger equation. Notably, our approach provides the widest range of $Q_0$ values (i.e., the range of values for the non-absorption coefficient) among known results for the 2D Helmholtz equation. Lastly, we discuss the limitations of our approach and possible ways to enhance existing inequalities. The Tsallis distribution can be interpreted through the lens of statistical mechanics, where it represents a deviation from entropy due to system constraints. In the realm of social systems, this distribution has emerged in studies of human behavior, yet its underlying dynamics lacks a clear explanation. We investigate the Tsallis distribution in collective decision making, where individuals randomly choose between two options with different probabilities, specifically in cases where the probability distribution does not align with Tsallis statistics. By applying the Tsallis entropy concept to this scenario, we find that the resulting distribution can be an non-Tsallisian mixture of distributions. Furthermore, we determine the conditions under which the Tsallis-like distribution may arise, which includes deviations from the expected behavior and can be characterized by an index that reflects the complexity of the system. We also analyze possible connections between this index and the notion of overfitting. Ultimately, our research provides a straightforward explanation for the observed Tsallis distribution in the context of individual choice, thereby bypassing the need for more intricate interpretations. We also demonstrate that this Tsallisian phenomenon can extend beyond decision making to other aspects of social systems. Consequently, our findings offer a unified framework that encompasses various phenomena exhibiting Tsallis distribution-like characteristics. We further explore the limitations of our model by conducting multiple statistical tests and examining its robustness in the face of varying parameters. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for understanding the dynamics of social systems and provide a framework for extending and adapting our research to various real-world applications. We also offer the code used in this study to facilitate further research and replication of results. We propose that the index we derived holds significant potential for assessing the complexity of real-world systems and their constituent parts, even in cases where explicit data may not be accessible. We believe that the methodology we employed is universally applicable to any phenomenon exhibiting a Tsallis distribution. We also explore the connection between our findings and the concept of entropy in the context of symbolic sequences. For classical and quantum systems, we develop a comprehensive framework of Hamiltonian dynamics within the context of quantum equilibrium states. Our approach identifies four distinct categories of Hamiltonian dynamics: (1) time-invariant Hamiltonian dynamics, (2) time-dependent Hamiltonian dynamics, (3) Hamiltonian dynamics generating quantum equilibrium states, and (4) Hamiltonian dynamics maintaining quantum equilibrium states. Our work, which draws upon existing results from quantum thermodynamics, includes the analysis of classical limit cases and provides examples of continuous-time quantum controllers. Furthermore, we demonstrate that under certain conditions, time-dependent Hamiltonian dynamics can generate quantum equilibrium states, leading to the quantum Jarzynski equality. Our framework and associated insights have implications for quantum thermodynamics and flux capacitor research. In contrast, a genuine negative temperature can be meaningfully applied to a two-level system, such as certain atomic or nuclear levels, offering a more precise analogy. A key characteristic of a two-level system with negative temperature is its ability to undergo spontaneous emission, a phenomenon typically associated with positive temperature. In a proposal for testing negative temperature, a suitable atomic system is identified, described by a specific energy level structure, and calculated to demonstrate the effect of temperature on its negative value. Furthermore, the impact of two-photon processes on its negative temperature can be investigated by utilizing this system in an optical cavity. A key aspect of this proposal involves presenting the two-level system's properties in a way that the effects of cavity coupling, driving, and dissipation on its negative temperature become clear. A coupled system like this, with the cavity coupled to an optical fiber, offers an additional advantage of providing insight into the spread of negative temperature to its surroundings. We introduce a minimal dark sector to extend the Standard Model, incorporating a scalar dark parity partner for the Standard Model fermions through a renormalizable interaction in a consistent dark parity framework. This minimal expansion allows us to analyze the stability of the vacuum in a two-loop scenario, which is otherwise compromised due to the negative mass terms induced by dark parity violation. Furthermore, this model serves as an expansion of the well-known linear and nonlinear seesaw frameworks, surpassing their predictive power by filling out the fundamental fermion mass matrices. The combination of dark parity symmetry and minimal expansion enables us to explore the scalar partner mass patterns and, in turn, the fundamental fermion mass spectra with a precise understanding of the dark sector's impact. We demonstrate that the consistent extension not only accurately reproduces the observed fundamental fermion masses but also provides a comprehensive framework that can be further expanded to accommodate dark matter phenomena. The model's distinctive features include the generation of mass hierarchies, the precise determination of the dark scalar partner masses, and the prediction of additional dark sector particles awaiting discovery at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). The successful incorporation of the minimal dark sector into the Standard Model through a renormalizable interaction paves the way for the development of a full-fledged dark sector motivated by the principles of dark parity symmetry, which can be tested through both phenomenological analyses and future particle physics experiments. The model's predictive capability is demonstrated by the computation of masses of additional scalar particles that could arise from an extension of the minimal dark sector, which are within the reach of the High-Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC). The predicted mass ranges for the additional scalar particles are: 700--1100 GeV for the minimal expansion of the standard model fermion family, 480--750 GeV for the minimal expansion of the third fermion family, and 2200--3300 GeV for the minimal expansion of the top quark fermion family. The model's consistency with the 125 GeV Higgs boson mass is verified through the computation of one-loop corrections to the Higgs boson self-energy in the minimal expansion of the Standard Model. The predicted mass ranges for the additional scalar particles can be verified through future LHC experiments at the HL-LHC. A key aspect of transition metal oxides is the spin-orbit coupling, and its strength can vary significantly, depending on whether electronic or lattice degrees of freedom are considered. In this study, effective spin-orbit coupling is examined in $f$ and $d$ electron systems, with the aim of identifying it as a emergent phenomenon resulting from interaction effects and crystal field splitting. For the case of $d$ electrons, an explicit expression is derived for the spin-orbit coupling, which is found to be proportional to the square of the 10d orbital component and dependent on the crystal field splitting. In cuprates, this leads to a hierarchical organization of spin-orbit coupling, crystal field splitting, and electron-electron interaction, and as a result, the effective Hamiltonian is found to be described by an easy-axis scenario with marginal spin-orbit coupling. In tartines, on the other hand, the spin-orbit coupling is found to be strong and delocalized, and it plays a crucial role in the physics of this material. Moreover, the derivation of the effective Hamiltonian is extended to the case of $f$ electron systems, and it is found that the spin-orbit coupling is the dominant interaction, and as such, the effective Hamiltonian can be described by an easy-axis scenario. Notably, the spin-orbit coupling in these systems differs from that found in rare-earth metals and rare-earth based compounds, which is typically strong and localized, and thus they are distinguished as having "weak spin-orbit coupling" character. Finally, the relevance of this approach is demonstrated in the case of NdTaO$_3$, where the effective Hamiltonian obtained through this method is compared to that obtained experimentally through the analysis of the spin wave dispersion. The outcome of this investigation underscores the generality of this approach in transitioning from the microscopic to the effective level. The emergence of easy-axis behavior in certain transition metal oxides is further substantiated by the comprehensive theoretical and experimental analysis of Ba$_2$CuSi$_2$O$_7$, where the easy-axis nature of the spin-orbit coupled Cu$^{2+}$ ions is confirmed through the direct observation of the zero-field spin noise spectrum. The outcome of this research opens up new avenues for exploring the physics of transition metal oxides with spin-orbit coupling, and it has a broader impact on understanding easy-axis behavior in general. This involves examining sub lattices of the weight lattice where the weights correlate with the exponents of the relative $I$-functions. For varieties defined by hypersurfaces within toric varieties, we demonstrate the connection between the relative $I$-functions and the Milnor lattices from local topological monodromy. Furthermore, we show that the relative $I$-functions of toric complete intersections with smooth divisors share a proportional relationship. This means that the ratio of two such $I$-functions is equivalent to the ratio of the volumes of the underlying varieties' sub lattices. This is particularly notable for varieties with irreducible components whose corresponding weights exhibit a high degree of symmetry. Using generative adversarial networks, we can create realistic representations of internal images corresponding to specific disease symptoms. However, altering the latent code is challenging due to the complex learned representations. We propose a method to easily modify the latent code in a Generative Adversarial Network, which significantly reduces the number of required training data samples by $2-5$. This approach enables us to change the generated image without significantly decreasing the quality. We apply this method to modify CT images featuring pulmonary nodules, which are critical for assessing cancer progression and nodule development. By manipulating the latent code, we can re-generate images showing NAC (no action cancer) patients who were incorrectly classified as having viable cancer cells. Consequently, this technique has potential uses in fake positive case analysis and development of more robust GAN representations. We also introduce a metric to evaluate the consistency of GAN representations when the latent code is altered. This metric assesses the agreement between different generated images representing the same medical condition. We utilize this metric to evaluate our method's effectiveness in maintaining representation consistency when the latent code is changed. We anticipate that this approach and proposed metric will contribute to the analysis of GAN representations in medical imaging. We demonstrate our method's applicability on two datasets: LIDC-IDX featuring pulmonary nodules and Pancreatic Cancer Imaging Dataset Analysis (PICIA), which features pancreatic cancer segments. We leverage these datasets to evaluate our approach and proposed metric, which we term the Consistency Loss Difference (CLD). The CLD measures the difference in loss between the original GAN representation and the one obtained using our approach, which we term the Encoded Representation GAN (ERGAN). We find that our method successfully encodes pancreatic cancer segments with a low CLD value $0.08 \pm 0.03$. We also find that ERGAN representations are less prone to fake positive case re-generation with a decrease of $13\%$ in correct classifications when the code is altered. We anticipate that our approach and proposed metric will facilitate the development of more robust GAN representations in medical imaging. We make our approach, ERGAN, and CLD metric publicly available to encourage further analysis of GAN representations in medical imaging. We also contribute the code used in this study to the community. We intend this contribution to facilitate widespread adoption of unsupervised learning in medical imaging analysis. advanced techniques such as t-SNE dimension reduction and a layered view to
present data in a clear and user-friendly manner. Users can explore the
visualized data by moving a marker along a variable, which the system then
uses to filter the dataset accordingly. Additionally, ViDaExpert includes a
feature for comparing two datasets of the same type by displaying them side
by side. This tool was created with the aim of assisting researchers,
particularly graduate students, in visualizing and comparing datasets for
their research projects, by simplifying the complex process of data
examination. ViDaExpert is an Excel-based add-in that can be downloaded from
